human_review: [test/e2e_node/testdeviceplugin/device-plugin.go] This looks like a workaround to me. The real issue seems to be how device manager considers itself healthy or not. [Here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.0-beta.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/plugin/v1beta1/server.go#L60) for example it's stated that "A server is considered healthy till an actual error occurs.", which is a dangerous sign in my opinion and can potentially be a reason for the flake. A server shouldn't be considered healthy at least up until it [starts listening on the registration socket](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.0-beta.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/plugin/v1beta1/server.go#L108), I guess.

[test/e2e_node/testdeviceplugin/device-plugin.go] we recently fixed error when kubelet was not considered healthy and watchdog killed it before it fully started: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135153

I don't think it will make sense to introduce "initialization" stage. So realistically the best we can do is to retry here.
[test/e2e_node/testdeviceplugin/device-plugin.go] test servers may be surpisingly slow. Typical timeouts are in minutes. Perhaps use `f.Timeouts.PodStart, f.Timeouts.Poll`
[test/e2e_node/testdeviceplugin/device-plugin.go] Done, thanks for the pointer.
[test/e2e_node/testdeviceplugin/device-plugin.go] I tend to agree that adding stages is both nontrivial and with uncertain ROI
[test/e2e_node/testdeviceplugin/device-plugin.go] @ffromani , now that the code freeze is over, does this seem like a legitimate e2e test hardening approach?
this lgtm, I would suggest to make timeouts longer though

title: add ReplicaSetFailedPodsBackoff: limit pod creation when kubelet fails ReplicaSet pods
human_review:
[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] It would be helpful to look at how other pod-creating controllers handle backoff in failure cases when the kubelet rejects a pod. For example:

Daemonset controller:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/efac8fdea24d37aa86b1fd72f526e3f0acaf9e13/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L805-L825

Job controller (I'm not sure if this handles the case where kubelet rejects pods):
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/efac8fdea24d37aa86b1fd72f526e3f0acaf9e13/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L901C31-L912

What do other pod-creating controllers (like statefulset) do? Should we make a distinct special behavior for replicaset controller, or try to do something common?

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] #### StatefulSet

StatefulSet has the same problem as ReplicaSet. It goes into a hotloop here

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/efac8fdea24d37aa86b1fd72f526e3f0acaf9e13/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L378-L386

One advantage is, that it does not pollute the cluster with failed pods, so the problem is not as noticeable. But it is a strain on resources...

I think we could easily solve this with a backoff, same as we do in the DaemonSet.

#### Job

I think we do not have to solve this problem for a Job. The Job will usually just finish faster after going over a certain number of failures (BackoffLimit, and other fields...). It would still be useful to have a  `ReschedulePodsOnKubeletRejection` feature here in the future though.

#### ReplicaSet

The difference from StatefulSet/DaemonSet is that we do not have a pod identity that we could use to base the backoff on. We only see that either a portion or all of the created replicas are failing. If we base the backoff on any failing pod, we would have scaling speed issues. So we need a custom backoff which I tried to explain in the code comments.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] > Job
>  It would still be useful to have a ReschedulePodsOnKubeletRejection feature here in the future though.

Actually, for Job we already have a mechanism to throttle pod re-creation in case of failed pods - we count the number of failed pods since the last successful pod, and backoff exponentially with base 10s (so the delays are 10s, 20s, 40), see [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#pod-backoff-failure-policy) and [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9acdca64e03d48f95da6f289ae18872f368f27b3/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1695). So, it is not clear to me what would be the benefit of `ReschedulePodsOnKubeletRejection` in Job.

btw, I think 10s is too much of a base delay, but that's another discussion :).

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] > So, it is not clear to me what would be the benefit of ReschedulePodsOnKubeletRejection in Job.

The backoff is only applicable for jobs with `.spec.backoffLimitPerIndex`, right? (updated my comment above). But even in that case `ReschedulePodsOnKubeletRejection` would still help as it would not fail the pod at all and just reschedule it to a better node.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] > The backoff is only applicable for jobs with .spec.backoffLimitPerIndex, right?

Actually. the backoff delay applies both for classical "backoffLimit" and "backoffLimitPerIndex". The only difference is that for "backoffLimitPerIndex" the scope of counting the number of failed pods since the last successful is within the index.
- [classical backoff](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/336a32a270997731873b6d8b616f4ae91d903fcf/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1695)
- [per index backoff](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/336a32a270997731873b6d8b616f4ae91d903fcf/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1820)
[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Nice, thanks for the explanation.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Definitely agree with Jordan and Michał here, rather than introducing a new mechanism we should ensure that the controller can safely create pods. It seems like the same mechanism should also be applied in StatefulSets, but there it will only apply to case where we allow parallel pod creation, which doesn't wait for previous pods to be running.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] After a SIG Apps discussion, we will try to make the proportional backoff part of the `slowStartBatch` function and look back at the pods that have been created.
[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] And then attempt a similar fix in StatefulSets.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] This will require some testing, but from my local tests creating 200 replicas RS takes up to 10s:
```
I0317 19:12:43.159542       1 replica_set.go:779] ">>> slowStartBatch is starting..." logger="replicaset-controller" count=200
I0317 19:12:43.159579       1 replica_set.go:783] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" batchSize=1 remaining=200

I0317 19:12:43.197996       1 replica_set.go:783] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" batchSize=4 remaining=197
I0317 19:12:43.202078       1 replica_set.go:783] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" batchSize=8 remaining=193
I0317 19:12:43.206846       1 replica_set.go:783] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" batchSize=16 remaining=185
I0317 19:12:43.414170       1 replica_set.go:783] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" batchSize=32 remaining=169
I0317 19:12:44.460584       1 request.go:752] "Waited before sending request" logger="replicaset-controller" delay="1.046108269s" reason="client-side throttling, not priority and fairness" verb="POST" URL="https://172.18.0.2:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods"
I0317 19:12:45.063424       1 replica_set.go:783] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" batchSize=64 remaining=137
I0317 19:12:48.314100       1 replica_set.go:783] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" batchSize=73 remaining=73
I0317 19:12:52.015248       1 replica_set.go:803] ">>> slowStartBatch ..." logger="replicaset-controller" succeeded=200
```
logs added for clarity in `slowStartBatch` [method](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/917a5569810e626f20b06951ed0e3cbf9b618470/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L778-L802), which is responsible for creating pods in batches (starting with 1, and every successful create allows us to double the batch size, up to 500 limit in a single batch). 

The discussion during today's sig-apps focus on expanding that method with the ability to periodically (every n-th iteration, not to overwhelm the creation with those checks) check the state of created pods, and eventually do not allow the doubling to happen (`slowStartBatch` will not double if we encounter an error). [Currently only api errors when creating pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/917a5569810e626f20b06951ed0e3cbf9b618470/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L600-L608) are the trigger for stopping the increased creations. We propose to expand that with pod status checks, which should allow us to also slow down the failure rate, if something like that happens. 

This will not resolve the issue, but our goal is to slow down the problem so that other tools (monitoring, primarily) could notice an increase in the pod creation and react to the problem. Rather than allowing an avalanche of bad pods trashing the cluster.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] I have experimented with an alternative solution and detect the failures in the slowStartBatch function. Please see the code in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131050, but have found couple of problesms.

We do not have a good controll over the backoff. When we try to create pods in some capacity and observe them fail, the new pods can trigger RS resync via the update handler before the RS backoff kicks in. And this new sync can create new pods again. Basically we can get into a loop as well. The bigger the ReplicaSet and the kubelet/scheduler delay, the bigger the chance of running into it. 

The reasons for the loop are:
- It can potentially take a long time before we get from Pending -> Failed.
- We observe updates from pods that land on the good nodes.
- When we get to the pod GC, each pod deletion can trigger the RS sync as well.

Also for small replica sets, it is hard to preserve the backoff since we always reset it to 0 because we are unable to detect the failures in a single sync.

It seems the best solution is to first do a lookback and decide how many pods should have failed per unit of time before we start creating new pods as proposed in the the current PR. Please let me know if you have a better idea on how to do the lookback.

I could also make the lookback part of the slowStartBatch, but then we run into the problem of polluting the log with

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ee41b03416ffe7e1e81d06d44aa02f5d9712b7dc/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L589-L590

since we can create no pods in empty syncs.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] > It seems the best solution is to first do a lookback and decide how many pods should have failed per unit of time before we start creating new pods as proposed in the the current PR. Please let me know if you have a better idea on how to do the lookback.
> 
> I could also make the lookback part of the slowStartBatch, but then we run into the problem of polluting the log with

The lookback being part of the `slowStartBatch`, to be exact [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0afe2b839d44383da7cc4e5bb48f873f17a939e5/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L602-L610) seems like a reasonable approach. Especially that [recently we've added a pod indexer](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130961) which will ensure that the pod listing and filtering the failed shouldn't be too heavy. 

So your proposed solution from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131050/ (assuming you'll use `rsc.getRSPods(rs)`) is the right path forward. Also, to eliminate looping through the pod list too many times, I'd suggest to do both the failed and starttime filtering in a single go.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Okay, make sense. I will make the lookback part of the slowStartBatch.
- it will be more responsive
- we need to do the first check even before creating the first pod
-  I will try to use the backoff mechanism from this PR (as mentioned the one in [#131050](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131050) does not work)

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] This is to limit the absolute number of pods to create in a single burst if we observe failing replicas. We could limit this even further. By a half sounds as a good compromise.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] - failed pods will limit the creation of new pods (e.g. weight 1)
- pods that failed in the current slowStartBatch execution have double the weight
[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Nit: can you comment what this value stands for. Also, maybe something like `FailedPodsWindow` or something more descriptive will be a better name.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Why do we need a feature gate? If you want to go with a [feature gate](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/feature-gates.md#features-which-do-not-change-the-api) you'll need to open a KEP and go through the entire graduation and release process. Because every FG is automatically a user-facing change, in this case it's the `--feature-gate` value that is to be configured by the cluster admin. 

Rarely, we decide to go with feature gates for bug fixes, and this particular case is no different. I've thought about it for a bit yesterday, and I think we can safely assume this is fixing a bug, so the surface is small, and with sufficient tests ensuring that both the error path isn't worse than before, and the "happy path" is the same I think we can just proceed with just controller changes.

Unless I missed something, did I?

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Let's extract the precondition function as a type:
```golang
type batchPreconditionFunc  func(successes int) (int, error)
```
and make sure to properly document the inputs and outputs, this will make the code easier to follow.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] I did some more testing and carefully reviewing this code and I have to admit that this is unnecessarily complicating the replica set controller, weaving the backoff calculations deeply inside the controller (see the below piece around `calculateTimeWeightedFailedPodsCount`) and the usual mechanism which we have inside the queue, which in case of failures  puts a particular RS in a queue rate limited, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/caa9324842e8f96702661505226a2c97ef62742f/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L559-L566

I would like to be able to re-use just that mechanism to slow down the creations, rather than introduce yet another one. To achieve that, I'm proposing:
1. Modify `slowStartBatch` function similarly to what you're doing here, introducing the `batchPrecondition` check. It will look like this `batchPrecondition func(successes int) error`. It accepts a number of successes and returns an error.  This function implementation will be very simpler version of what you coded in this PR:
    - Count failed pods in the last unit of time, the hardcoded 20 min might be too long, so I'm open to suggestions. I was personally thinking about 5 min for starters, or we can try to get that information from the queue, and modify the window based on `NumRequeue`, for example. 
    - If the number of failed pods is significantly exceeding the successes (I'm open to any particular implementation here, as long as the precondition function will be idempotent), return error stating that we're failing to create.
2. Inside `slowStartBatch` I'd invoke the function and break the loop every time the precondition returns an error. This will cause `manageReplicas` to finish with an error which will trigger the default backoff to kick in, the one I pointed above.
[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Drop these changes entirely, and rely on the fact that `manageReplicas` should return error and fall back to the default rate limited re-queuing.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] I'd like to re-use the default re-queuing mechanism, which already supports rate limiting, rather than introducing entirely new mechanism. See my other comment where I'm laying out what it should look like, and drop this entire piece of code.
[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Ack, renamed to BurstFailedPodWindow and added comments.

[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] We most likely do not need a FG for this bug fix. I originally added it to allow people to disable the feature in case we introduce a regression.

I removed the FG, let's see if we can simplify the fix.
[pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go] Please see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130411#issuecomment-3612187122

title: Migrate RoleBinding.RoleRef to +k8s:immutable declarative validation
human_review:
[staging/src/k8s.io/api/rbac/v1alpha1/types.go] If we are already here, Can you add required also?
`// +k8s:required`

[pkg/registry/rbac/rolebinding/declarative_validation_test.go] Also add tests for 
1. set -> unset("")
2. unset("")-> set

[staging/src/k8s.io/api/rbac/v1alpha1/types.go] Unfortunately `+k8s:required` cannot be used on non-pointer struct fields. When I tried adding it, the validation codegen fails with:

```
field k8s.io/api/rbac/v1.RoleBinding.roleRef: tag "k8s:required": non-pointer structs cannot use the "k8s:required" tag
```

This is because `RoleRef` is declared as `RoleRef RoleRef` (a value type), not `*RoleRef` (a pointer). The `+k8s:required` tag is only meaningful for pointer types where nil indicates "not set". For non-pointer structs, the field always has a value (the zero struct), so `+k8s:required` doesn't apply.

The existing `// +required` marker (OpenAPI) is already present and correct for documentation/schema purposes.

[pkg/registry/rbac/rolebinding/declarative_validation_test.go] I explored adding these test cases, but they hit pre-existing DV mismatches that are outside the scope of this PR:

When `RoleRef` is set to the zero value (empty struct `RoleRef{}`), the **create-time** validation fires additional errors:
- `roleRef.apiGroup` is not `"rbac.authorization.k8s.io"` (it's `""`)
- `roleRef.kind` is not a supported value (it's `""`)
- `roleRef.name` is required (it's `""`)

These create-time validation rules are not yet migrated to DV, so the equivalence check (`VerifyUpdateValidationEquivalence`) fails with `apiserver_validation_declarative_validation_mismatch_total` metric errors — the handwritten validation produces errors that the declarative validation doesn't (or vice versa).

The `+k8s:immutable` migration itself is correctly validated by the existing "roleRef changed" test case (which changes from one valid `RoleRef` to another valid `RoleRef`). The zero-value transitions would effectively be testing the not-yet-migrated create validations rather than the immutability check.

Once those create-time validations are migrated to DV in a future PR, the zero-value test cases will become feasible to add.
[staging/src/k8s.io/api/rbac/v1alpha1/types.go] I see, Somehow I was thinking RoleRef is a type of string.

[pkg/registry/rbac/rolebinding/declarative_validation_test.go] Thanks for the detailed explanation! You're right - I've now:

1. Modified `ValidateRoleBindingUpdate` to check immutability **first** and short-circuit (skip RoleRef field validation) when roleRef changes, matching the DV early-return behavior.
2. Extracted a `validateRoleRef` helper to share between `ValidateRoleBinding`, `ValidateRoleBindingUpdate`, and `ValidateClusterRoleBinding`.
3. Added both test cases: `set -> zero value` and `zero value -> set`.

All DV equivalence tests pass across all 3 API versions and all 4 feature gate scenarios.
It is a pretty solid PR.  Minor comments to increase the coverage of DV.

title: cel: add allContainers() helper to access all pod containers in a single list
human_review:
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/pod_test.go] PodSpec is also embedded in workload types such as Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob,  ReplicaSet, and PodTemplate. 

Tests that ensure all workload types work as expected will be essential.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/pod.go] If the field is present is must be a slice. I would expect an error here if it's not.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/environment/base.go] ```suggestion
		IntroducedVersion: version.MajorMinor(1, 37),
```

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/pod.go] What alternatives were considered?

Off the top of my head I could imagine some other formulations such as:

- `object.spec.allContainers().all(c, c.image.startsWith('myregistry.io/'))`
- `object.spec.allContainers(c, c.image.startsWith('myregistry.io/'))`

Why was `allContainers(<spec>)` selected over the alternatives considered?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/pod.go] There is a complication I'd like to make sure is fully considered: containers and initContainers share `v1.Container` but use it differently (e.g. initContainers use `restartPolicy: Always` to register a sidecar).  Also, ephemeralContainers has it's own dedicated type (`v1.EphemeralContainer).

This has a lot of subtle implications.  For example, a CEL rule that requires livenessProbes would seem to work when first introduced but would make it impossible for a client to add an ephemeralContainer because ephemeralContainers don't have a field for livenessProbe.

I'm not comfortable allowing users to define CEL rules that seems to work for containers but then break in when used with ephemeralContainers because I'm not convinced developers will think to test this case.

One possible way to address this would be to find a common subset of fields that all containers share and only allow access to those fields via this library.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/pod.go] I don't think this warning needs to be included here.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/cost.go] Please add corresponding cost tests.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/pod.go] Yeah, a few alternatives we can try:

1. allContainers(<spec>) (current)
2. object.spec.allContainers() --> method-style on the spec
3. object.spec.allContainers(c, c.image.startsWith(...)) --> macro-style with predicate

We went with form (1) for these reasons:

a. Consistency with the existing apiserver CEL library. Existing helpers (check(), fieldSelector(), labelSelector(), semver(), ip(), cidr()…) are all free functions taking the target as an argument rather than receiver methods. allContainers(<spec>) fits the same shape.

b. The receiver method (form 2) requires a typed receiver. object.spec in MAP/VAP / CRD validation is dyn, so binding .allContainers() to a PodSpec-typed receiver isn't straightforward. Binding it as a universal method on dyn risks collisions and surprises users in contexts where .spec isn't a PodSpec at all. A free function taking dyn is explicit about "treat this argument as a pod spec shape."

c. Macro-style with predicate (form 3) loses composability. Returning a list lets callers layer any existing list macro / method on top .all(), .exists(), .filter(), .size(), .map(), the new two-variable comprehensions, etc. A baked-in predicate form would need to be duplicated for each use case, and users lose the ability to, e.g., compute allContainers(spec).size() or intersect two predicates.

Happy to revisit if form (2) is strongly preferred, the implementation is essentially the same. I would want to understand how it interacts with dyn receivers before committing.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/pod.go] Thanks for raising this, it's a real footgun. You're right: even though Container and EphemeralContainerCommon structurally carry the same fields in the Go types, the API validator rejects ports, livenessProbe, readinessProbe, startupProbe, and lifecycle on ephemeral containers, and init containers have sidecar-specific semantics around restartPolicy. A CEL rule author writing allContainers(spec).all(c, c.livenessProbe.httpGet.path.startsWith("/healthz")) would get silent acceptance at rule-write time and blocking validation errors later when somebody tries to attach an ephemeral container.

Options I see, roughly in order of scope:

1. Document the limitation in the godoc and let users opt into narrower helpers (initContainers, containers, ephemeralContainers) when they need fields outside the common subset. Cheapest, but relies on the author's reading the doc.

2. Return views restricted to the common-subset fields (your suggestion). The list returned by allContainers would expose only fields valid on all three kinds: name, image, command, args, workingDir, env, envFrom, resources, volumeMounts, volumeDevices, terminationMessagePath, terminationMessagePolicy, imagePullPolicy, securityContext, stdin, stdinOnce, tty, restartPolicy, resizePolicy. Fields not in the common set would be absent on all elements (so a reference would error consistently rather than working-then-breaking). This gives authors a hard guarantee.

3. Split the helper into commonContainers(spec) (common subset) and kind-specific accessors. More ceremony, but makes the tradeoff explicit in the name.

I lean toward (2) as the option that best matches your intent. The implementation means wrapping each container in a thin traits.Indexer/traits. Mapper view that projects only the allowed keys doable without a schema, since the allow-list is a static set of field names.

One subtlety: if we go with (2), we should make sure object.spec.containers[0].livenessProbe remains reachable via the original path we would only be restricting what allContainers(...) exposes. Authors can still drill into containers specifically when they need kind-specific fields.

Would you like me to prototype (2) in this PR, or pause the PR while we settle the shape of the common view (and potentially coordinate with @lalitc375 and sig-api-machinery)?

human_review:
[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] Nit:

[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] To make the test slightly more robust - would it make sense to embed `t` in the mock plugin here and run `t.Fatalf` whenever any of the Pods passed as QPIs is not contained in `p.order`?

[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] Currently, the test relies on kube-scheduler shutting down before `pod-a` can successfully bind. If, for some reason, the context cancellation takes too long to propagate, `pod-a` might successfully bind to `node-preferred` before scheduler's shutdown completes.

In such case, the test would still pass but for a wrong reason - `pod-b` will be scheduled to `node-other` simply because `pod-a` is already bound and consuming its capacity, completely bypassing the NNN logic that this test intends to exercise.

To prevent such false positives, could we add an explicit assertion below here that checks that `pod-a` got the NNN equal to `node-preferred` but didn't actually get scheduled there (i.e. Pod's `spec.NodeName` field is empty)?

[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] > the context cancellation takes too long to propagate

I believe cancelling the context will synchronously propagate the cancellation to all children. Bind will see that its context is cancelled and fail any new outbound requests (including the bind request), unless it somehow uses a context that doesn't descend from the scheduler's context.

That said, it may be worth having a confidence check regardless. With the current setup, it's difficult to check if a pod really didn't get scheduled, as there can be arbitrary delay between the binding request and actuation.

I think the most robust way to ensure that the pod doesn't get bound is to replace the default binding plugin.

[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] Actually, could we run `t.Errorf` instead and add some safe fall backs in both `Less` and `Bind`?

The problem is that `t.Fatalf` should be run from the main test goroutine exclusively - apparently, calling it from a background goroutine does not stop the test - instead, it silently terminates only that specific background goroutine.
[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] SGTM, I guess that you can now safely assert that the `NodeName` field is indeed empty right after here :)

[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] Consistency nit: let's either add analogous assertions for `*mockPreBindPlugin` and `*mockQueueSortPlugin` or drop it for `*mockBindPlugin`.
[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] Nit: apparently, `t` is not needed anymore?

[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] Do you think it's still worth checking? We replaced the binding plugin so we have good reason to assume NodeName isn't set, and if NNN is empty the test will fail later. I'd prefer to avoid polling to assert that NodeName isn't set.

[test/integration/scheduler/nominated_node_name/nominated_node_name_test.go] Polling isn't necessary here anymore, particularly due to your mock binding plugin. A single Get request is sufficient to verify that `NodeName` is empty and the NNN is set appropriately.

In addition:
- This is a nice way to document how the system is expected to behave here,
- The entire purpose of this test is to ensure that the scheduler respects the NNN logic across restarts; as previously pointed out, if the Pod accidentally binds for any reason (e.g. a future regression in the scheduler framework that somehow bypasses the mock binding plugin), the test will still pass because of a wrong reason. [staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/cel/errors.go] Yes, CEL evaluation errors are scheduling errors. Users will see the enhanced error message (with the hint) in two places:

### 1. Pod Conditions (`kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`)

```
Conditions:
  Type:       Scheduled
  Status:      False
  Reason:      SchedulerError
  Message:      class gpu-class: selector #0: CEL runtime error: no such key: sharingStrategy.
                Consider using CEL optional chaining (?), has() macro, or orValue() for optional fields
```

**Code path**: `handleSchedulingFailure` → `updatePod()` → `v1.PodCondition{Message: errMsg}`

### 2. Events (`kubectl get events --field-selector involvedPod.name=<pod-name>`)

```
LAST SEEN   TYPE      REASON              MESSAGE
...
1m          Warning   FailedScheduling   class gpu-class: selector #0: CEL runtime error: no such key: sharingStrategy.
                                 Consider using CEL optional chaining (?), has() macro, or orValue() for optional fields
```

**Code path**: `handleSchedulingFailure` → `EventRecorder().Eventf(pod, ..., "FailedScheduling", errMsg)`

---

## Error Propagation Chain

The CEL error message (with the hint) is preserved through the following chain:

```
CEL Runtime Error → cel.EnhanceRuntimeError()
  → selectorsMatch() → allocateOne() → Allocate()
  → DynamicResources.Filter() → fwk.AsStatus(err)
  → findNodesThatPassFilters() [via errCh.SendWithCancel → errCh.Receive]
  → findNodesThatFitPod() → schedulePod() → schedulingCycle()
  → handleSchedulingFailure() → status.Message()
  → User (via Pod Condition & Event)
```

Key point: CEL errors have `status.Code() == fwk.Error`, so they take the `fwk.AsStatus(err)` path (not `fwk.Unschedulable`), and the complete error message including the hint is preserved and displayed via `status.Message()`.

[staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go] # Design Discussion: Device ID Placement in Error Messages

## Summary

We've implemented adding device ID to CEL runtime error messages as requested by the TODO comment. Before finalizing this implementation, we'd like to get feedback on the architectural design decision.

## Implementation

**Current change:**
```go
// Before:
return false, fmt.Errorf("class %s: selector #%d: CEL runtime error: %w", class.Name, i, err)

// After:
return false, fmt.Errorf("class %s: selector #%d on device %q: CEL runtime error: %w", class.Name, i, deviceID.String(), err)
```

This allows users to identify which specific device triggered the error.

## Design Question

We have a question about the **appropriate layer** for adding device context.

### Observation

The `deviceID` consists of three parts:
- `Driver`: Used by CEL as default domain for attribute name resolution
- `Pool`: Used only for device identification
- `Device`: Used only for device identification

**Key insight**: CEL evaluation only needs `Driver` for attribute resolution, but our error message includes all three parts (`driver/pool/device`).

### Why This Makes Sense

We see two abstraction layers here:

1. **CEL evaluation layer**: Device is "anonymous" - only attributes matter
   - Like SQL `WHERE age > 18` doesn't care about row ID
2. **Scheduler layer**: Device has identity (driver/pool/device)
   - Needs to track which specific device failed

The error is wrapped at the CEL evaluation layer (`selectorsMatch`), but includes device context because that's where the error occurs. This is the narrowest scope that still has device context available.

### Alternative: Wrap at Scheduler Layer

We considered wrapping errors at the scheduler layer (`isSelectable` call sites). This would:
- ✅ Make all device-related errors consistent
- ✅ Keep CEL errors pure (no device context)

However, there are **three types of errors** in `selectorsMatch`:

1. **CEL compile error** - No device ID needed (user code issue, not device-specific)
2. **Device conversion error** - Could benefit from device ID
3. **CEL runtime error** - Needs device ID (our change)

If we wrap at the scheduler layer, compile errors would incorrectly include device ID:
```
device "gpu.nvidia.com/pool-0/gpu-0": class gpu-class: selector #0: CEL compile error: syntax error
```

This doesn't make sense because compile errors are problems with the CEL expression itself, not specific to any device.

## Our Questions

1. **Is the current approach acceptable?**
   - We add device ID at the CEL evaluation layer for runtime errors only
   - Different error types have different context levels

2. **Should we also add device ID to conversion errors?**
   ```go
   if err := draapi.Convert_api_Device_To_v1_Device(device, &d, nil); err != nil {
       return false, fmt.Errorf("convert device %q: %w", deviceID.String(), err)
   }
   ```

3. **Should we refactor to wrap at scheduler layer with selective unwrapping?**
   - This would require error type detection to exclude compile errors
   - More complex but potentially more consistent

## Current Implementation

For now, we've implemented the minimal change that addresses the TODO:
- ✅ Adds device ID to CEL runtime errors
- ✅ Removes the TODO comment
- ✅ Helps users identify which specific device failed
- ✅ Maintains distinction: compile errors (no device) vs runtime errors (with device)

We believe this is the narrowest appropriate scope for adding device context. Would you like us to proceed with this approach, or would you prefer a different design?

## Example

**Before**:
```
class gpu-class: selector #0: CEL runtime error: no such key: sharingStrategy. consider using CEL optional chaining...
```

**After**:
```
class gpu-class: selector #0 on device "gpu.nvidia.com/gpu-pool/gpu-0": CEL runtime error: no such key: sharingStrategy. consider using CEL optional chaining...
```

[staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go] > Is the current approach acceptable?

Yes, makes sense to me. One nit: use `%s` instead of `%q` in the error string. Error strings often get shown as quoted strings, which means that the embedded double quotes need to be escaped. This is less readable. We don't need to worry about spaces or empty strings here, so `%s` is fine.

> Should we also add device ID to conversion errors?

Yes, let's do that, even if it's "just in case" and for consistency. In practice that conversion should never fail.

> Should we refactor to wrap at scheduler layer with selective unwrapping?

No.

human_review: [test/e2e/framework/test_context.go] I'm still wondering if list-tests is better than a ginkgo dry-run ... feels like we're re-inventing the wheel in an incompatible way.
[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] not sure why we need a global here, versus just building up a set of unique labels when traversing a tree of featuregates ?
[test/e2e/framework/test_context.go] They are not mutually exclusive, just different. You don't get an easily diff-able one-line-per-test output from `--dry-run`.
[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] This is the intermediate attempt to collect all feature gate tags across different nodes. The next commit removes this again and is entirely local to the method.

[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] The code currently adds all dependencies. In the case of DRA that means that it adds `Feature:DynamicResourceAllocation` although that feature gate is on-by-default and GA. I'm undecided whether we want that.
[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] Once we know what we want I'll update the unit tests for this code - they are currently failing and don't cover the new scenarios.
[test/e2e/apimachinery/mutatingadmissionpolicy.go] The first commit is something that I could pull out into a separate PR.

[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] I'm undecided whether it is worth moving these additional labels to the end of the node text right now. It adds some churn (https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22974890/unify-tags.txt) and only helps in a few cases:

```
auth/projected_clustertrustbundle.go:266: [sig-auth] [FeatureGate:ClusterTrustBundle] [Beta] [Feature:OffByDefault] [FeatureGate:ClusterTrustBundleProjection] [Beta] [Feature:OffByDefault] should be able to mount a big number (>100) of CTBs + [BetaOffByDefault]
     ->
auth/projected_clustertrustbundle.go:266: [sig-auth] [FeatureGate:ClusterTrustBundle] [FeatureGate:ClusterTrustBundleProjection] [Beta] [Feature:OffByDefault] should be able to mount a big number (>100) of CTBs + [BetaOffByDefault]
```

What I'd like to achieve is:
- Meta tags (Slow/Serial/Alpha/Beta/Disruptive/Flaky/OffByDefault) appear once at the end of the full test name. It is convenient that they can be added in e.g. a Context call, but showing them in the middle of the test name makes those less readable.
- Feature and FeatureGate get inserted where called. They can be a significant part of the test name ("[Feature:Foo] must work"). FeatureGate is eventually going away, but then it can be replaced with plain text.

Agreed?

But without this, where do we want the feature gate dependencies? Directly after the feature gate which causes them, potentially multiple times and repeating the Alpha/Beta of the dependencies?
[test/e2e/apimachinery/mutatingadmissionpolicy.go] => https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134703

[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] XREF: I'm experimenting with moving the tags to the end of test names in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134708.

We can continue to discuss here what we want to achieve.

[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] > What I'd like to achieve is: [...]

I was intentionally more conservative when adding labeling and tried to preserve the exact same test names as before due to concerns that jobs could break which match those test names. I think we have enough experience with labeling now that we can be confident that it works. Any job that breaks because of  some old FOCUS/SKIP should be converted to labels.

Having said that, I consider moving those meta labels as unlikely to break jobs because the regexps which relied on them already had to be very flexible and handle different positions and ordering.

[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] This text is no longer necessary because usage of normal `ginkgo.It` is fine because of changes already made for Kubernetes 1.36.

Because we no longer need it, feature gates can use a separate featureGate struct more easily (no need to replicate this explanation).
[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] I'm not a fan of recursion, specially on this kind of code that depends a lot on humans doing the right thing,

[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] Are you worried about cycles? What this handles is the data built into the default feature gate, not some user-supplied data. If this doesn't finish, we'll know before a PR gets merged because this code runs each time e2e.test is invoked.

[test/e2e/framework/ginkgowrapper.go] Cycle detection isn't dependent on recursion or not anyhow (can be implemented either way), and I don't think moving this to an explicit stack would improve readability or reliability. We don't need to micro-optimize this.
Just for a quick sanity check I want to confirm some of the alpha + beta test outputs but this LGTM

What I want to understand is WHY this is correct.

If I found a Deferred validation which specifically asks for ParentContext, why is it OK to just convert that to ThisContext?  On the surface that seems wrong, so please analyze and explain why it is correct and safe -- how could one end up in this situation?  

Here's how I understand it, please tell me if I am wrong.

Consider a case like:

```
// +k8s:item(key: "x")=+k8s:childTag1
// +k8s:item(key: "x")=+k8s:childTag2
```

Assume childTag1 produces a Function("abc") and a Deferred("def"), while childTag2 produces a Function("xyz").

There are two ways to interpret that:

Simple: We don't accumulate item calls per criteria, so "deferred" really has no meaning here.  Handling the first tag-line, we would call "abc" followed by "def", and then we would do the second tag-line and call "xyz".

Correct: We accumulate item calls per criteria, so "deferred" means "after all non-deferred tags for this criteria".  We would have to collect "abc" and "xyz", keyed by the criteria, and then do "def" after both of those.

IMO, the "correct" approach is correct, but I am not convinced it will actually matter, and we probably should not waste time on it.

Assuming my assessment is close to correct - this is the sort of comment I want - the full analysis.  This way, some future you or me who realizes we actually do need to accumulate will remember WHY we did it this way -- not because it was Correct but because it was Good Enough.

+# EndpointSlice Consumer Helpers
+
+This package provides helper functions for consuming EndpointSlices in Kubernetes.
+
+## Overview
+
+The EndpointSlice API is the mechanism that Kubernetes uses to let Services scale to handle large numbers of backends. However, working with EndpointSlices directly can be challenging because a single Service may have multiple EndpointSlice objects, and endpoints can move between slices.
+
+This package provides helper functions that make it easier to consume EndpointSlices by:
+
+1. Providing a unified view of all EndpointSlices for a service across multiple EndpointSlice objects
+2. Handling the complexity of tracking EndpointSlice additions, updates, and deletions
+3. Offering informer-like and lister-like interfaces that are familiar to Kubernetes developers
+
+## Components
+
+### EndpointSliceConsumer
+
+The `EndpointSliceConsumer` is the core component that tracks EndpointSlices and provides a unified view for a service. It is kept up-to-date via `OnEndpointSliceAdd`, `OnEndpointSliceUpdate`, and `OnEndpointSliceDelete` callbacks (typically wired up via an informer).
+
+```go
+// Create a new consumer
+c := consumer.NewEndpointSliceConsumer()
+
+// Add an event handler
+c.AddEventHandler(consumer.EndpointChangeHandlerFunc(func(serviceNN types.NamespacedName, slices []*discovery.EndpointSlice) {
+    fmt.Printf("Service %s/%s has %d slices\n", serviceNN.Namespace, serviceNN.Name, len(slices))
+}))
+
+// Get all EndpointSlices for a service
+slices := c.GetEndpointSlices(types.NamespacedName{Namespace: "default", Name: "my-service"})
+```
+
+### EndpointSliceInformer
+
+The `EndpointSliceInformer` provides an informer-like interface for EndpointSlices that handles tracking multiple slices for the same service.
+
+```go
+// Create a new informer
+informer := consumer.NewEndpointSliceInformer(informerFactory)
+
+// Add an event handler
+informer.AddEventHandler(consumer.EndpointChangeHandlerFunc(func(serviceNN types.NamespacedName, slices []*discovery.EndpointSlice) {
+    klog.InfoS("Service endpoints changed", "namespace", serviceNN.Namespace, "name", serviceNN.Name, "slices", len(slices))
+}))
+
+// Start the informer
+if err := informer.Run(ctx); err != nil {
+    klog.ErrorS(err, "Failed to run EndpointSliceInformer")
+    return
+}
+
+// Get all EndpointSlices for a service
+slices := informer.GetEndpointSlices(types.NamespacedName{Namespace: "default", Name: "my-service"})
+```
+
+### EndpointSliceLister
+
+The `EndpointSliceLister` provides a lister-like interface for EndpointSlices that allows listing slices for a given service by label.
+
+```go
+// Create a new lister
+lister := consumer.NewEndpointSliceLister(endpointSliceLister)
+
+// Get all EndpointSlices for a service
+slices, err := lister.EndpointSlices("default").Get("my-service")
+if err != nil {
+    klog.ErrorS(err, "Failed to get EndpointSlices")
+    return
+}
+```
+
+## Migrating from Endpoints to EndpointSlices
+
+This package is designed to help applications migrate from using the Endpoints API to using the EndpointSlices API. The interfaces provided by this package are similar to those used with Endpoints, making the migration easier.
+
+When migrating from Endpoints to EndpointSlices, consider the following:
+
+1. EndpointSlices are more scalable than Endpoints, especially for services with a large number of backends
+2. EndpointSlices provide more information about endpoints, such as topology hints and node names
+3. Each EndpointSlice carries its own `Ports` field; consumers that need to associate ports with endpoints should iterate over `GetEndpointSlices` rather than flattening all endpoints into a single list
+4. EndpointSlices are the preferred way to access endpoint information in Kubernetes

+// EndpointSliceConsumer provides a unified view of endpoints for services
+// across multiple EndpointSlice objects.
+type EndpointSliceConsumer struct {
+	// lock protects slicesByService.
+	lock sync.RWMutex
+
+	// slicesByService maps service namespaced names to a map of EndpointSlices
+	// keyed by their names.
+	slicesByService map[types.NamespacedName]map[string]*discovery.EndpointSlice
+
+	// handlers for endpoint changes
+	handlers []EndpointChangeHandler
+}
+
+// EndpointChangeHandler is called when endpoints for a service change.
+type EndpointChangeHandler interface {
+	// OnEndpointsChange is called when endpoints for a service change.
+	OnEndpointsChange(serviceNN types.NamespacedName, endpoints []*discovery.EndpointSlice)
+}
+
+// EndpointChangeHandlerFunc is a function that implements EndpointChangeHandler.
+type EndpointChangeHandlerFunc func(serviceNN types.NamespacedName, endpoints []*discovery.EndpointSlice)
+
+// OnEndpointsChange calls the function.
+func (f EndpointChangeHandlerFunc) OnEndpointsChange(serviceNN types.NamespacedName, endpoints []*discovery.EndpointSlice) {
+	f(serviceNN, endpoints)
+}
+
+// NewEndpointSliceConsumer creates a new EndpointSliceConsumer.
+func NewEndpointSliceConsumer() *EndpointSliceConsumer {
+	return &EndpointSliceConsumer{
+		slicesByService: make(map[types.NamespacedName]map[string]*discovery.EndpointSlice),
+	}
+}
+
+// AddEventHandler adds a handler for endpoint changes.
+func (c *EndpointSliceConsumer) AddEventHandler(handler EndpointChangeHandler) {
+	c.lock.Lock()
+	defer c.lock.Unlock()
+	c.handlers = append(c.handlers, handler)
+}
+
+// OnEndpointSliceAdd is called when an EndpointSlice is added.
+func (c *EndpointSliceConsumer) OnEndpointSliceAdd(endpointSlice *discovery.EndpointSlice) {
+	serviceNN, sliceName, ok := endpointSliceCacheKeys(endpointSlice)
+	if !ok {
+		return
+	}
+
+	c.lock.Lock()
+	defer c.lock.Unlock()
+
+	slices, ok := c.slicesByService[serviceNN]
+	if !ok {
+		slices = make(map[string]*discovery.EndpointSlice)
+		c.slicesByService[serviceNN] = slices
+	}
+
+	// Check if this is a new slice or an update to an existing one
+	existingSlice, exists := slices[sliceName]
+	slices[sliceName] = endpointSlice.DeepCopy()
+
+	// Only notify handlers if this is a new slice or the endpoints have changed
+	if !exists || !reflect.DeepEqual(existingSlice.Endpoints, endpointSlice.Endpoints) {
+		c.notifyHandlersLocked(serviceNN)
+	}
+}
+
+// OnEndpointSliceUpdate is called when an EndpointSlice is updated.
+func (c *EndpointSliceConsumer) OnEndpointSliceUpdate(_, newEndpointSlice *discovery.EndpointSlice) {
+	c.OnEndpointSliceAdd(newEndpointSlice)
+}
+
+// OnEndpointSliceDelete is called when an EndpointSlice is deleted.
+func (c *EndpointSliceConsumer) OnEndpointSliceDelete(endpointSlice *discovery.EndpointSlice) {
+	serviceNN, sliceName, ok := endpointSliceCacheKeys(endpointSlice)
+	if !ok {
+		return
+	}
+
+	c.lock.Lock()
+	defer c.lock.Unlock()
+
+	slices, ok := c.slicesByService[serviceNN]
+	if !ok {
+		return
+	}
+
+	if _, exists := slices[sliceName]; exists {
+		delete(slices, sliceName)
+		if len(slices) == 0 {
+			delete(c.slicesByService, serviceNN)
+		}
+		c.notifyHandlersLocked(serviceNN)
+	}
+}

human_review: [test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] why doing it in defer? Can we wait for delete as part of a regular test flow so we are not required to understand the order of AfterEach and defers?

[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] couldn't we also register this as an JustAfterEach? I think it's more idiomatic ginkgo and would take care of the defer. we could branch on whether createdPod was nil to skip in case the test is skipped before we create the pod.

Another option may be a DeferCleanup()

[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] Sorry, I was sick. I switched it to `DeferCleanup()`, it has the advantage that if the test fails, the defer will run anyways and so the kubelet can be restarted.

@haircommander @SergeyKanzhelev thanks!
[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] let's pass delete option with grace period = 0 so it will be faster
[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] the Pod will not be around after `DeleteSync`. Why we need this check?

[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] I really worried about this approach. Is the approach of having a finalizer on a Pod and wait for terminal status reported by the kubelet before setting finalizer work?
[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] Added, thanks!

[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] `DeleteSync()` just waits synchronously until the pod is deleted from the API server. It basically calls [WaitForPodNotFoundInNamespace](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bc15d50fd246bef83aa9b00fcc475d1959296294/test/e2e/framework/pod/pod_client.go#L239) that just does a [get](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bc15d50fd246bef83aa9b00fcc475d1959296294/test/e2e/framework/pod/wait.go#L674) in a loop until the API server returns nil. It's just a busy loop polling until the pod is not returned by the apiserver.

That is not enough, as we need to wait until the kubelet removes the pod dir. And that doesn't happen when the kubelet deletes the pod, as the [pod dir removal is left for the periodic cleanup](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bc15d50fd246bef83aa9b00fcc475d1959296294/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2583).

The approach I took is to use this existing helper, to wait until all containers are removed in the node first (`waitForAllContainerRemoval()` queries the runtime to check when that the containers were actually removed). Once that happens, wait until the pod directory is removed.

We can just wait until the pod directory is removed, without waiting for container removal, that should work anyways. It felt simpler to wait more "step by step", but we can remove this and just wait for the pod directory being removed.

[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] Nope, I don't think that will help. A finalizer would hold the API server object alive until the kubelet reports terminal status, but as I mentioned in the previous comment, the kubelet deletes the pod but leaves the pod dir to be removed "lazily", in the next iteration of periodic cleanup function.
[test/e2e_node/user_namespaces_test.go] I've removed the `waitForAllContainerRemoval()` and just left the wait for the pod dir to be removed and updated the comment. Let me know what you think
@SergeyKanzhelev thanks, PTAL :)

/lgtm
/approve

+	clientset "k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes"
+	"k8s.io/client-go/rest"
+	utiltesting "k8s.io/client-go/util/testing"
+	kubeapiservertesting "k8s.io/kubernetes/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/testing"
+	"k8s.io/kubernetes/test/integration/framework"
+	"k8s.io/kubernetes/test/utils"
+)
+
+var (
+	auditPolicy = `
+apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
+kind: Policy
+rules:
+  - level: Request
+    resources:
+    - group: ""
+      resources: ["pods"]
+    verbs: ["get"]
+`
+)
+
+func TestCerts(t *testing.T) {
+	logFile, err := os.CreateTemp("", "audit.log")
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("Failed to create audit log file: %v", err)
+	}
+	defer utiltesting.CloseAndRemove(t, logFile)
+
+	policyFile, err := os.CreateTemp("", "audit-policy.yaml")
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("Failed to create audit policy file: %v", err)
+	}
+	if _, err := policyFile.Write([]byte(auditPolicy)); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("Failed to write audit policy file: %v", err)
+	}
+
+	s := kubeapiservertesting.StartTestServerOrDie(t, kubeapiservertesting.NewDefaultTestServerOptions(), []string{
+		"--audit-policy-file", policyFile.Name(),
+		"--audit-log-version", "audit.k8s.io/v1",
+		"--audit-log-mode", "blocking",
+		"--audit-log-path", logFile.Name(),
+	}, framework.SharedEtcd())
+	defer s.TearDownFn()
+
+	// Generate self-signed certificate
+	key, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	keyRaw, err := x509.MarshalECPrivateKey(key)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	serialNumberLimit := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), 128)
+	serialNumber, err := rand.Int(rand.Reader, serialNumberLimit)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	commonName := "test-cn"
+	notBefore := time.Now().Truncate(time.Second)
+	notAfter := notBefore.Add(time.Hour)
+	cert := &x509.Certificate{
+		SerialNumber: serialNumber,
+		Subject:      pkix.Name{CommonName: commonName},
+		NotBefore:    notBefore,
+		NotAfter:     notAfter,
+
+		KeyUsage:              x509.KeyUsageKeyEncipherment | x509.KeyUsageDigitalSignature,
+		ExtKeyUsage:           []x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageClientAuth},
+		BasicConstraintsValid: true,
+	}
+	certRaw, err := x509.CreateCertificate(rand.Reader, cert, cert, key.Public(), key)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+
+	// Use self-signed certificate in client config
+	clientConfig := rest.CopyConfig(s.ClientConfig)
+	clientConfig.BearerToken = ""
+	clientConfig.CertData = pem.EncodeToMemory(&pem.Block{Type: "CERTIFICATE", Bytes: certRaw})
+	clientConfig.KeyData = pem.EncodeToMemory(&pem.Block{Type: "PRIVATE KEY", Bytes: keyRaw})
+	client, err := clientset.NewForConfig(clientConfig)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("error occurred: %v", err)
+	}
+
+	// Make a request using the client
+	podName := "foobar"
+	currentTime := time.Now().Truncate(time.Second)
+	_, err = client.CoreV1().Pods("default").Get(context.TODO(), podName, metav1.GetOptions{})
+	if err == nil {
+		t.Fatal("expected error, but it was nil")
+	}
+
+	// Verify that audit log has the expected entry
+	stream, err := os.OpenFile(logFile.Name(), os.O_RDWR, 0600)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Errorf("unexpected error: %v", err)
+	}
+	defer stream.Close()
+
+	annotationDetails := fmt.Sprintf(`certificate "%s" [client] issuer="<self>" (%s to %s (now=%s)) failed: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority`, commonName, notBefore.UTC(), notAfter.UTC(), currentTime.UTC())
+	expectedEvents := []utils.AuditEvent{
+		{
+			Level:      auditinternal.LevelRequest,
+			Stage:      auditinternal.StageResponseStarted,
+			RequestURI: fmt.Sprintf("/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/%s", podName),
+			Verb:       "get",
+			Resource:   "pods",
+			Namespace:  "default",
+			Code:       401,
+			CustomAuditAnnotations: map[string]string{
+				kubex509.CertificateErrorAuditAnnotation: annotationDetails,
+			},
+		},
+	}
+
+	auditAnnotationFilter := func(key, val string) bool {
+		return key == kubex509.CertificateErrorAuditAnnotation
+	}
+
+	missing, err := utils.CheckAuditLinesFiltered(stream, expectedEvents, auditv1.SchemeGroupVersion, auditAnnotationFilter)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Errorf("unexpected error checking audit lines: %v", err)
+	}
+	if len(missing.MissingEvents) > 0 {
+		t.Errorf("failed to get expected events -- missing: %s", missing)
+	}
+}

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] Need an integration test to show that all the wiring actually works.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] `GetHumanCertDetail` might be better, though it could make the audit log large?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] Not sure if we need rate limiting on this to prevent audit log spam if a broken client is hot looping requests.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] Perhaps `GetPrivateCertDetail` to underline that it contains sensitive data?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] We're not issuing a new audit log event, this merely updates the existing one
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] `GetHumanCertDetail` is an existing function in `k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/dynamiccertificates`.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] I know that, you are still increasing the size of audit events.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] Oh, I see, got it. Using it now - although I had to update it to truncate current time to seconds to pass unit tests (not before and not after are already being displayed like that now)
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] Ah, we can truncate CN and Issuer CN in `GetHumanCertDetail` to avoid audit log growing too large, WDYT?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] Not sure what you mean - we need this context so that `AddAuditAnnotation` would store annotations in it

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] I definitely don't think we want all the detail / size of GetHumanCertDetail ... it looks pretty unbounded and includes a bunch of stuff irrelevant to cert validation.

At *most*, length-limited versions of the issuer and the subject CN would be what we'd want to add to figure out what cert failed authentication.

Questions I have:
- if a client makes a request which contains an unacceptable client-cert AND a valid bearer token, will this check the cert, fail, audit-log the cert details, then validate the token, authenticate the request, and result in an audit event with `authentication.k8s.io/certificate-error` annotations that actually succeeded?
- I don't have a firm handle on the exposure implications of logging issuer / subject for failed requests ... maybe folks on some of the cluster provider security teams could weigh in on whether adding this is desirable or not (cc @micahhausler @ahmedtd @vinayakankugoyal for input)

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] I'm not sure why are we concerned about the size of audit log event - users can enable `audit-log-truncate-enabled` and tweak it with `audit-log-truncate-max-event-size` setting.

>if a client makes a request which contains an unacceptable client-cert AND a valid bearer token, will this check the cert, fail, audit-log the cert details, then validate the token, authenticate the request, and result in an audit event with authentication.k8s.io/certificate-error annotations that actually succeeded?

Yes, iiuc `unionAuthRequestHandler` will pass it to the next handler. I think its desirable as it the only way I can think of to notify admins that certificate has expired / no longer valid

>I don't have a firm handle on the exposure implications of logging issuer / subject for failed requests

Note that "logging" is a good word here - we're not storing certificate details in kube-apiserver logs, we're keeping them alongside other important private info - source IPs, query args for requests, sometimes even entire request / responses etc.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] > I'm not sure why are we concerned about the size of audit log event - users can enable audit-log-truncate-enabled and tweak it with audit-log-truncate-max-event-size setting.

The annotations field in the audit event says values should be short, and we pay serialization cost for excessively large values even if we then truncate them. If this PR is intended to assist admins in finding invalid certificates, let's just pick a reasonable bound to prevent abuse and truncate the issuer and subject CN.

> Yes, iiuc unionAuthRequestHandler will pass it to the next handler. I think its desirable as it the only way I can think of to notify admins that certificate has expired / no longer valid

If the request is actually failing as a result, including the issuer/subject CN of a presented client cert is *probably* ok? If the request actually succeeded, it's pretty weird to do. I'd still like feedback from the folks mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130540/files#r2058912959 on how concerning it is to log the issuer / subject of every unknown cert we encounter

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] My calculations for maximum length of this string: `max length(common name) + len("usages, serving") + len(" groups[]") + max length(organization) + len(" validServingFor=[]") + 3 * max length(domain defined attribute value length for IP) + 3 * max length(domain defined attribute value length for DNS names) + len(" issuer=") + len(" ( to  (now=))") + 3*timestamp` based on RFC3280  assuming that the certificate has 3 IPs and 3 DNS names. `64 + 16 + 10 + 64 + 20 + 384 + 384 + 9 + 15 + 90` makes `1056`, so it should be safe to truncate the annotation to 1024 (we may cut part of current time, which isn't crucial since audit event will have the timestamp anyway). WDYT?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] we probably don't need anything but the issuer and subject common names for identifying the certificate, the SANs / groups / timestamps seem less relevant for figuring out what client has the failing cert

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/request/x509/x509.go] ah yes, I started with that in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/7d29cf0e078aea1ad1b87939cd1edb7468abd5c8 and then Mo recommended reusing `GetHumanCertDetail`. I'll update it to use custom function and limit it to 512 to fit serial number and two common names

[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/cel/library.go] https://github.com/google/cel-go/releases/tag/v0.27.0

Guessing this change is for this bit in the release notes:

> ⚠ Breaking Changes
>
> Remove types as variables: The logic for handling types has been relaxed to support safe rollout of feature packages which introduce new types whose names may collide with existing variables. Please review your policies if you relied on types behaving strictly as variables in previous versions. PR #1262

The related [PR](https://github.com/google/cel-go/pull/1262) says

> Allow user-defined variables to shadow type variables.

Does this mean any previously persisted CEL expressions using types as variables will still resolve those but via a different path (enabling shadowing), or that they will now fail compilation?

Do we want to add a unit test that demonstrates such a use, to sanity check it still behaves like it did previously?

cc @jpbetz @TristonianJones

[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/checker/scopes.go] I'm not sure of all the ways resolution happens, but fields whose names start with `.` remain addressable via `['.name']` syntax, right? Do we have test coverage for that?  Same question below.
[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/checker/scopes.go] Do spurious `.` prefixes (like `object..field` or `.object`) still fail properly with the trimming applied in various places?
[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/interpreter/attribute_patterns.go] As far I can tell, k8s always type-check CEL expressions, so this is not used for the moment.

[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/cel/library.go] This is a change to better support the introduction of new CEL types in a forward compatible way.

For example, if K8s has a variable named `resource` and an opaque type were introduced with the same name by CEL later on, the K8s type for `resource` would be preserved and override the CEL type introduced in the library.

[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/checker/scopes.go] The leading '.' has a very specific meaning in CEL which indicates that the identifier should not be resolved within a container or alias, but should be used as-is. This would allow you to say something like the following:

```go
env, _ := cel.NewEnv(cel.Variable('x', cel.MapType(cel.StringType, cel.StringType)))
env.Compile('x.exists(x, x == .x.y)')
```

It's an odd statement to make, but allows for references to variables at the top scope while if they get shadowed in a comprehension.

[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/ext/regex.go] This is the first introduction of the regex libraries to core CEL, so they came with costs out of the box. Not every library had this (such as strings, we're fixing this now) and so we introduced cost changes as a version bump if the extensions didn't come with costs from the get-go
[vendor/github.com/google/cel-go/interpreter/attribute_patterns.go] It's highly unlikely this would affect you since it's only hit on parse-only paths.

[test/e2e/node/pod_resize.go] If I understand correctly, we hit infeasible only when the request is greater than the total node allocatable.

Here for example

Total node available CPU: 100%
1. Pod 1: 50% of node available CPU
2. Pod 2: 25% of node available CPU
3. Pod 3: 6.25% of available CPU

Current available CPU : 18.75%

Resize Pod 3 which already has 6.25% of available CPU to include current available CPU (18.75%) + 75% of Pod 1 (75% of 50 = 37.5%)
So total Pod 3 requirement is 18.75% + 37.5% = 56.25%

Pod 3 requirement: 56.25%
Current available: 18.75%
Pod 3 already have: 6.25%

Required for Pod 3 to be running 31.25% hence its moves in to deffered state.

Resize Pod 1 to 1/4th from initial value.
Initial value 50% CPU
After 1/4th resize, Pod 1 need: 12.5%, Given back to node allocatable: 37.5%

This makes the Pod 3 from deffered state to Running.

title: Handle HPA generation fields
human_review:
[pkg/registry/autoscaling/horizontalpodautoscaler/strategy.go] The generation increment here is not gated behind `HPAGeneration`, unlike `PrepareForCreate`. When the gate is disabled, create leaves `Generation=0`, but the first spec update unconditionally sets it to `1` (`0+1`). The gate effectively provides no protection.

Either gate this path too, or (preferably) consider dropping the gate entirely — every other resource that manages generation does so unconditionally (Deployment, StatefulSet, ReplicaSet, Job, CronJob, Ingress, DaemonSet, PodDisruptionBudget, etc.).

[pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go] `setStatus` unconditionally sets `ObservedGeneration` without checking the `HPAGeneration` feature gate. When the gate is disabled and `Generation` is `0` (its zero value), this sets `ObservedGeneration = &int64(0)`, which differs from the previous `nil`. This will trigger a spurious status update for **every** HPA on the first reconciliation cycle after upgrade, even when the feature is supposedly disabled.

This should either be gated, or the feature gate should be removed (see my other comment on `strategy.go`).

[pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go] Other Kubernetes controllers simply assign `ObservedGeneration = object.Generation` after reconciliation (StatefulSet, ReplicaSet, DaemonSet, Deployment, etc.). For instance [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L574). The `max()` here is defensively correct given that `setStatus` reconstructs the entire status struct from scratch, but it would be worth a comment explaining why this differs from the standard pattern.

In practice, `hpa.Generation` is the generation of the object the controller just reconciled, so `max()` shouldn't make a difference — if it ever did, it might mask a real bug (e.g. processing a stale informer cache entry).

[pkg/registry/autoscaling/horizontalpodautoscaler/strategy_test.go] Nit: the error message reports `hpa.Generation` (the old, pre-update HPA) instead of `hpaUpdated.Generation`.

```suggestion
				t.Error("Expected generation to be ", tc.expectedGenerationOnUpdate, ", got ", hpaUpdated.Generation)
```

[pkg/features/kube_features.go] Nit: `Generation` lives in `metadata`, not `spec`. Suggest:
```suggestion
	// Enables generation tracking for HorizontalPodAutoscaler
```

/lgtm

Thanks a lot!

title: cli-runtime/printers: fix column alignment regression from periodic tabwriter flush
human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go] `len(...)` measures bytes, not displayed character width. `text/tabwriter` computes widths in terms of runes (and may differ from UTF-8 byte length), so this padding can be incorrect for non-ASCII cell values or header names, reintroducing misalignment. Consider using rune-count-based width calculation (e.g., `utf8.RuneCountInString`) consistently for both `maxCellWidths` and `len(name)` (and ensure it matches whatever width logic tabwriter uses)."

[staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go] `len(...)` measures bytes, not displayed character width. `text/tabwriter` computes widths in terms of runes (and may differ from UTF-8 byte length), so this padding can be incorrect for non-ASCII cell values or header names, reintroducing misalignment. Consider using rune-count-based width calculation (e.g., `utf8.RuneCountInString`) consistently for both `maxCellWidths` and `len(name)` (and ensure it matches whatever width logic tabwriter uses)."

[staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go] This fix only primes widths when headers are printed (`!options.NoHeaders`). With `--no-headers`, the first periodic flush still happens after row 100 and can still lock in narrower widths than later rows, so misalignment across flush groups can persist. To fully fix the regression, consider priming widths even without headers (e.g., by pre-padding the first written row’s non-final columns, or writing a synthetic priming line to the tabwriter before streaming rows).

[staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter_test.go] The test hard-codes assumptions about the periodic flush interval (`flushInterval=100`) but doesn’t actually reference the production value. If the flush interval changes (or becomes configurable), this test can become ineffective (e.g., if the interval increases beyond `rowCount`, the regression won’t be exercised). If the interval is a package constant, consider basing `rowCount` on that constant (e.g., `2*flushInterval + ...`) so the test reliably spans multiple flush groups.

[staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go] `fmt.Sprint(cell)` allocates a new string for every non-string cell during the pre-scan. On large tables with many non-string cells, this can noticeably increase CPU and allocations beyond what’s necessary just to compute widths. If this shows up in benchmarks, consider a type switch for common scalar types (int, int64, float64, time.Duration, etc.) using `strconv`/specialized formatting into a small scratch buffer to compute length without allocating a new string each time.

[staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go] maxCellWidths is computed from len(s)/len(fmt.Sprint(cell)), but the actual bytes written for a cell can be different due to truncation at \f/\n/\r (adds "...") and escaping of \x1b ("^["), which can *increase* the rendered width. If a later flush group contains one of these values, the first flush may still latch a too-small width and misalignment can persist. Consider computing the displayed width using the same rules as appendCellValue (truncate index + 3, plus ESC expansion) so the pre-scan matches what tabwriter will actually see.

[staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go] The full-table pre-scan runs for every table whenever output is a tabwriter (PrintObj wraps outputs in a tabwriter), even when len(table.Rows) <= flushInterval and no periodic flush will occur before the final Flush. In those cases tabwriter will already compute widths over the whole output, so the extra pass is unnecessary overhead. Consider gating the pre-scan/priming logic on whether periodic flushing will actually happen (e.g., len(table.Rows) > flushInterval).

[staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go] bytes.Repeat allocates a new slice of length pad each time it's called. If a column has a very large max width, this can create a large transient allocation just to emit spaces (header) / append padding (first row). Consider writing padding from a small reusable buffer (e.g., a fixed "spaces" array written in chunks) to avoid O(pad) temporary allocations.

## Pull request overview > [!NOTE] > Copilot was unable to run its full agentic suite in this review. Fixes a column-alignment regression in `printTable` when periodic `tabwriter` flushes occur before the widest cell value is seen, by priming tabwriter column widths up-front and adding a regression test. **Changes:** - Pre-scan table rows to compute per-column max widths and pad headers so the first periodic flush latches correct widths. - Preserve periodic flushing behavior to keep memory bounded. - Add a regression test asserting consistent column start offsets across flush groups. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 2 out of 2 changed files in this pull request and generated 5 comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter.go | Pre-scans row cell widths and pads header columns to avoid misalignment across periodic tabwriter flushes. | | staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/printers/tableprinter_test.go | Adds a regression test validating that column boundaries remain aligned across flush boundaries. | --- 💡 Add Copilot custom instructions for smarter, more guided reviews. +// addOwner takes a package name (= import path, like k8s.io/client-go),
+// tries to look up the source code of the package, and then
+// walks up until it finds an OWNERS file with some sig label.
+// The first sig label found this way is used.
+//
+// If successful, that SIG gets added to the name.
+// If not, the name remains unchanged.
+func (p *packageOwners) addOwner(name string) string {
+	if p == nil {
+		return name
+	}
+
+	dir := p.pkgs[name]
+	if dir == "" {
+		// Look up via `go list`. To invoke it less often,
+		// we also ask for sub-packages and cache the results.
+		// We don't care about errors.
+		//
+		// This is roughly what golang.org/x/tools/go/packages does,
+		// which we can't use here because it would add a new
+		// dependency to k/k.
+		cmd := exec.Command("go", "list", "-f", "{{.ImportPath}}:{{.Dir}}", name+"/...")
+		out, _ := cmd.Output()
+		scanner := bufio.NewScanner(bytes.NewReader(out))
+		for scanner.Scan() {
+			line := scanner.Text()
+			parts := strings.SplitN(line, ":", 2)
+			if len(parts) != 2 {
+				continue
+			}
+			p.pkgs[parts[0]] = parts[1]
+		}
+		dir = p.pkgs[name]
+	}
+
+	// Walk up starting from an absolute path until we cannot go up further.
+	for ; dir != "" && dir != "." && dir != "/"; dir = path.Dir(dir) {
+		data, err := os.ReadFile(path.Join(dir, "OWNERS"))
+		if err != nil {
+			continue
+		}
+		var owners owners
+		if err := yaml.Unmarshal(data, &owners); err != nil {
+			continue
+		}
+		for _, label := range owners.Labels {
+			if strings.HasPrefix(label, "sig/") {
+				// Bingo!
+				return fmt.Sprintf("[sig-%s] %s", label[4:], name)
+			}
+		}
+	}
+
+	return name
+}
