human_review:
[test/e2e/node/pods.go] @dims do you understand the reason for it? I remember looking into it and I don't think we ever got to the root cause for it. Same as comment from @BenTheElder : https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/131605#issuecomment-3664982241

I am fine ignoring it. But understanding it will be great. For example, can `/bin/true` return `2`?

[test/e2e/node/pods.go] > fast-delete scenarios

there is no fast delete in test as I understand it. It is fast fail. But nothing makes it run faster or fail faster. It should just take it's time to get to the failure.

Should we say "fast fail" instead of "fast-delete" at a minimum?
[test/e2e/node/pods.go] seems like we should *really* understand why this increased in frequency significantly 5 days ago before we suppress it

[test/e2e/node/pods.go] @dims and @mikebrow looking into https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/13049

This PR is on hold to understand it
[test/e2e/node/pods.go] The real source of the exit code 2 is probably a pause container: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/build/pause/linux/pause.c#L58
[test/e2e/node/pods.go] The "fast delete" is the action in the podFastDeleteScenario: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/node/pods.go#L845

[test/e2e/node/pods.go] there's a working theory (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135713#issuecomment-4092666900) that when the stop races with the actual underlying `runc create`, an exit code of 2 can result

the PLEGOnDemand feature makes the kubelet react instantly to delete requests instead of coalescing them on a 2 second poll boundary, so makes a fast create-then-delete much more likely to translate into a race between runc creating and stopping the container

once we prove this is what is happening, tolerating a slightly different non-zero exit here seems ~ok to me (even if we want to pursue improving containerd / runc to produce a more consistent error code in that scenario)

[test/e2e/node/pods.go] it's looking more and more like runc handling of the term signal prior to handoff to the underlying process is the cause of the 2 exit code, I think this PR to add that to the list of non-zero exit codes we accept is fine.

Maybe also limit this to the `t.Message == ""` case? If some other non-empty message shows up that doesn't match this pattern, we don't want to ignore it

```suggestion
		case t.ExitCode == 2 && t.Reason == "Error" && t.Message == "":
```
[test/e2e/node/pods.go] let's also log that this is happening (similar to the reBug88766 logging below), and point to a specific runc issue with details
[test/e2e/node/pods.go] Fixed both @liggitt

[pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go] You are right, to handle init containers properly, I updated `validatePodScopeResources` to consider the two main stages:
1. Init containers: The sum of resources (CPU and Memory) from all guaranteed init restartable containers has to be smaller than the total amount of pod level resources, if there are any containers that require access to the podSharedPool. Also, it is needed to check if the largest non-restartable guaranteed init container fits in the remaining after subtracting all restartable containers (this check may be redundant, because of the admission checks).
1. Init restartable and Standard containers: The sum of (CPU and Memory) from all Guaranteed init restartable and standard containers has to be smaller than the total amount of pod level resources, if there are any containers that require access to the podSharedPool.

- A guaranteed container with its own cpu set
- A non-guaranteed container with a podSharedPool cpu set. 

So, we need to check if the container has an integer number of cpus (removed `cpuValue > 0`, IsContainerQOSGuaranteed already checks that), to verify that the container has an exclusive cpu set, that is not part of the podSharedPool.

For InPlacePodVerticalScaling, we overwrite the spec resources with the allocated resources after a new resize is accepted by the kubelet. This function is specifically intended to do that, if you look at the lines directly below you can see that we overwrite the container resources in the spec.

Are we supporting IPPR with this feature? I assume the answer is no, because neither PLR nor resource managers support IPPR at all today. [pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go] We have to consider the two different paths:
- `PodLevelResourceManagers` disabled:
   - Pod without `pod-level` resources:
      - With any container that has exclusive cpus, we can assume that they satisfy all the CPU manager requirements, so we can disable quota.
   - Pod with `pod-level` resources:
      - Not possible to have exclusive CPU sets.
- `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled:
   - Pod without `pod-level` resources:
      - With any container that has exclusive cpus, we can assume that they satisfy all the CPU manager requirements, so we can disable quota. Same as `'PodLevelResourceManagers' disabled`.
   - Pod with `pod-level` resources:
      - Exclusive containers: Satisfy guaranteed requirement on their own and integral request of CPU, and have exclusive cpu assignment, so we can disable quota.
      - Pod shared pool container: Do not satisfy guaranteed requirement on their own nor have integral request of CPU, however they still have the exclusive cpu assignment (the one that represents the pod shared pool), but we should not disable quota.

This is why we need to make the check for both container QoS-like and integral CPUs, so we can differentiate truly exclusive CPU sets, from pod shared pool CPU sets.

With the new CPU manager helper `ResourcesQualifyForExclusiveCPUs` function (checks for container QoS and integral CPU request), the logic can be like this:
```
if cpumanager.ResourcesQualifyForExclusiveCPUs(container) && containerHasExclusiveCPUs(cm.cpuManager, pod, container) {
```

[pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager/scope_container.go] > I am trying to recall if there was a reason we wanted to add an error message specifically for pods with pod-level resources.

The intention was to make easier to access and notice what was going on with the decisions from the resource managers, and to clearly transmit that the current logic would accept all pod-level pods without offering exclusive resource allocation (until the Pod Level Resource Manager feature is implemented).

> Do users benefit from knowing that the container scoped topology alignment failed for a pod with PLR?

Because of the QoS being determined solely by the pod-level resources and the new introduced hybrid model, the possible allowed pod specs can be more complex, and the `container` scope decisions are affected by the QoS defined with the pod-level resources. So I think it is helpful for the user to be specific in this scenario.

Besides, the current version admits all pod-level pods, and after upgrading any pod-level pod would be dependent on the admission logic from the resource managers (a currently accepted pod spec, could be rejected after upgrading and enabling this feature).

[pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/state/checkpoint.go] I agree that the JSON decoding is purely additive, however, adding fields to existing checkpoint structs breaks the checksum verification. 

The Kubelet verifies file integrity using `dump.ForHash(checkpointStruct)`, which includes all struct fields in its generated string representation (even empty/nil fields). If we add `PodEntries` to `V2`, any existing `V2` checkpoint file read from disk will fail checksum validation because `dump.ForHash()` will generate a different string than when the file was originally saved, triggering a `CorruptCheckpointError`.

/cc @ffromani

[pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/state/checkpoint.go] Before V3 was introduced, `CPUManagerCheckpointV2` was just the type alias for `CPUManagerCheckpoint`. The standard `checksum.New()` function uses the struct's type name when generating the hash.

After introducing V3, I turned `CPUManagerCheckpointV2` into its own distinct struct to preserve the old fields. Because the struct name changed from `CPUManagerCheckpoint` to `CPUManagerCheckpointV2`, the resulting hash also changed, even if the data inside was identical.

In summary, it is necessary because it gracefully handles both situations:
   1. `ck.Verify(cp)` succeeds: This handles the V2 checkpoints that were generated by a Kubelet using the new standalone `CPUManagerCheckpointV2` struct.
   2. The fallback `dump.ForHash` and `strings.Replace` succeeds: This handles truly legacy V2 checkpoints generated by older Kubelets where the struct was still named CPUManagerCheckpoint.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134768/commits/e503afeb321c0037542ffa94c2c9ef33d987f091#r2488825750 and following made me eventually realize the overarching issue and main pain point with the implementation. 

With pod-level resource managers and pod-level shared/exclusive resources, we are essentially introducing *a sub-pooling mechanism* and *a new level of isolation/exclusivity for resources*. These concept are emerged and explained in the KEP, but not explcitly and openly; for example, we didn't defined clearly new terms and described them indirectly rather than address these directly.

I think this is still fine, as the KEP did a good enough job describing the impact and the changes, and most notably these concepts emerge kinda naturally at *implementation* stage, is (still) not obvious these should be spelled out at user interface/API layer. The benefits of doing so are still unclear.

But at implementation layer these concepts are more relevant, because we need a higher level fo detail. Most of the confusion and the possible source of bugs (see comments about the recovery flow and the memory manager internal state) IMO stems from the fact we are trying to squash the third isolation level we are introducing in the existing two, but the model isn't really fit and breaks.

Previously, a resource (CPU, memory) could have been allocated like this

| shared | isolation level | exclusive? |
| ---------  | --------------------- | ------------- |
| yes       | host                   | no             |
| no         | container         | at container level |

Now we have  

| shared | isolation level | exclusive? |
| ---------  | --------------------- | ------------- |
| yes       | host                   | no             |
| **pod** | **pod** | **within the pod** |
| no         | container         | at container level |

And this should be exposed by resource managers. Previously `GetExclusiveCPUs` could safely return a boolean (binary state). 

| shared | isolation level | `GetExclusiveCPUs() returns` | `GetResourceIsolationLevel() returns` |
| ---------  | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| yes       | host                   | `false`       | `Host`
| no         | container         | `true`         | `Container` |

To correctly and represent the new reality, we should probably add a `GetResourceIsolationLevel()` function, likely replacing `GetExclusiveCPUs` and/or reimplementing the latter in terms of the former to minimize the disruption radius. While refactoring is debatable, is now clear that we have flows, internal in the resource managers and related to the calling sites, where we need this extra level of granularity.

| shared | isolation level | exclusive? |`GetExclusiveCPUs() returns` | `GetResourceIsolationLevel() returns` |
| ---------  | --------------------- | ------------- |------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| yes       | host                   | no             | `false`                                         | `Host` |
| **pod** | **pod** | **within the pod** | `false` ???? to be decided | `Pod` |
| no         | container         | at container level | `true` | `Container` |

So, to wrap up, what we actually need here is again to expose the right abstraction layer rather than second-guess from the outside what the resource manager did or would do. With proper isolation layer acknowledged, tracked and reported, the code we are discussing about would devolve in a (IMO) crystal clear

```
func (cm *containerManagerImpl) ContainerHasExclusiveCPUs(pod *v1.Pod, container *v1.Container) bool {
	if resourcehelper.IsPodLevelResourcesSet(pod) && !utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(kubefeatures.PodLevelResourceManagers) {
		return false
	}
	return containerHasResourceIsolation(cm.cpuManager, pod, container, v1.ResourceCPU) == cmqos.IsolationContainer
}
```
(note this is made-up pseudocode example)
**IMPORTANT NOTE**: please don't rush to implement `GetResourceIsolationLevel`, it requires more thought. The _concept_ of the more granular isolation level, more granular than a bool, is IMO needed. The best way to represent it, especially within the current constraint, is not clear yet.

human_review:
[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/converter.go] This will overflow uint64 values > max int64 ... I'm not sure whether it is better to error or cast to a float64 in that case, but silently overflowing and going negative is definitely not what we want to do. Since going out to json and then back in would produce a float64, casting uint64 values > max int64 to float64 is probably better.

This should also add tests for the overflowing and non-overflowing cases to exercise the expected behavior.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/converter.go] I suggest we return error in this case, since float64 can only represent exact values up to `2^53`, casting uint64 to float64 also cause distortion.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/converter.go] > I suggest we return error in this case, since float64 can only represent exact values up to 2^53, casting uint64 to float64 also cause distortion.

I don't think this is the right layer to error on overflow errors ... the intent of this is to produce a `map[string]interface{}` that is equivalent to marshaling to json and then unmarshaling.

Something like this should accomplish that:

```go
case reflect.Uint8, reflect.Uint16, reflect.Uint32:
	realMap[fieldInfo.name] = int64(fv.Uint())
case reflect.Uint, reflect.Uint64:
	uintValue := fv.Uint()
	if uintValue <= math.MaxInt64 {
		realMap[fieldInfo.name] = int64(uintValue)
	} else {
		realMap[fieldInfo.name] = float64(uintValue)
	}

title: Fix create failed when resource required is zero
human_review: [pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] at first glance, we should handle this corner case earlier in the flow, possibly in `allocateContainerResources` before to call this function. And this case probably deserves a log line.
[pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] The issue arises here. The initial design intended to consider and handle various scenarios here, so it seems appropriate to address it here as well.
[pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] I agree the issue is raised here, but we should not try to even attempt allocation if we actually have no request. So we can handle this in the upper layer.
[pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] Should the pod be rejected by the API server if container requests <=0 devices?
[pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] Apiserver is more focused on the scheme, and configuring `0` does not violate this rule

[pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] It seems this change may inadvertently impact node reboot scenario, which was specifically addressed in [PR #114640](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114640).

Previously, we removed this check from `devicesToAllocate` to handle node reboots effectively. Since there’s no distinction between device allocation flows during a reboot versus normal operations, the scenario where `needed == 0` and node reboot happened, additional admission checks were introduced (in the aforementioned PR) to prevent runtime errors:

1. Device Plugin Re-registration: Ensure that the device plugin has re-registered with the kubelet and healthy devices are available on the node for allocation to recovered pods.

1. Device Health Verification: Confirm that previously allocated devices remain healthy post-reboot.

Without these checks, the recovery order of the device plugin pod and the application pod becomes critical. Since we have no control over the recovery order, devices might not be properly recovered. A pod might pass admission but fail at runtime by attempting to access a device that was never re-allocated, leading to runtime errors.

[pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] the judgment of `needed` here is different from the position of `needed` in the [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116376) deletion.

Here, `needed` refers to `resource.requests`, while in the PR, `needed` refers to the difference between `resource.request` and the number of `healthy devices`.

And the `needed` here is before `deviceToAllocate`. If the request is 0, there is no need to proceed with the allocation process, which can be traited as no devices being required.

The e2e tests had passed in the CI, and the tests designed in the [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116376) are also included.

[pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go] Thanks @yylt for pointing out that `needed` refers to resource.requests (which is same as resource.limit) here! That's a good point and definitely alleviates some of my concerns with this change. I will unhold the PR.

/unhold

We're actively working on improving this test through [#129010](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129010). @ffromani, it seems that we are unable to run the device reboot test in the presubmit job due to its flaky status. I’m happy to manually test it, and I believe @yylt might be willing to help as well, but I’m thinking long-term. If more such PRs are proposed, manual testing may not be sustainable and would likely become inefficient.

title: P&F: enable mutating work estimator
human_review:
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/apis/flowcontrol/bootstrap/default.go] There is a difference in the target namespace (`kube-system` vs. every) in the first resourceRule.

In both FlowSchemas, the first resourceRule casts a pretty wide net, catching more than leader elections.  If I understand correctly, doing leader elections with Endpoints or ConfigMap objects has been deprecated for a long time and not done by code in k/k.  If this is correct I would advocate removing the first resourceRule from both FlowSchemas.

The narrowness of the above remarks is not intended as a defense of the current suggested config.  I suggested a different set of config objects in the first place, and was never convinced that what we have now is better.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/apis/flowcontrol/bootstrap/default.go] > If I understand correctly, doing leader elections with Endpoints or ConfigMap objects has been deprecated for a long time and not done by code in k/k. If this is correct I would advocate removing the first resourceRule from both FlowSchemas.

We migrated all core components out of it (there are some out-of-tree components still using it, but that should motivate them to switch). So yes - I agree we should remove this part of rule.

I would even claim that we should cherrypick it back, as currently, we still have things like endpoint-controller that could starve leader-election.

Also - the namespace for the second rule (leases) is NamespaceEvery for both rules (not sure if it's desired or not). So this is why I would remove the second rule.
Alternatively, we can change to kube-system in the first one, but I'm not sure if having two rules it buys us anything,

@MikeSpreitzer - if/when we agree on that - I will open a separate PR for it, as this is independent bugfix to ahve.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/apis/flowcontrol/bootstrap/default.go] So:
- the main reason why this was needed to past test was that kubemark was actually still using Endpoints instead of EndpointsSlices - I addressed that in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106740
- I already have a separate PR where we're discussing this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106725

But for now, I'm going to revert this change and double run tests against the current state - which I believe should actually pass now at head, by just enabling this mutating estimator.

+func testPath(client clientset.Interface, path string, requiredChecks sets.String) error {
+	var result restclient.Result
+	err := wait.Poll(100*time.Millisecond, 30*time.Second, func() (bool, error) {
+		result = client.CoreV1().RESTClient().Get().RequestURI(path).Do(context.TODO())
+		status := 0
+		result.StatusCode(&status)
+		return status == 200, nil
+	})
+	if err != nil {
+		return err
+	}
+	body, err := result.Raw()
+	if err != nil {
+		return err
+	}
+	checks := sets.NewString(strings.Split(string(body), "\n")...)
+	if missing := requiredChecks.Difference(checks); missing.Len() > 0 {
+		return fmt.Errorf("missing required %s checks: %v in: %s", path, missing, string(body))
+	}
+	return nil

If reflective conversion didn't do this, and this isn't being called in generated code in this PR, why is it being added?

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go] Also potential to time travel without component restart if a new reflector is instantiated.

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go] @wojtek-t Instead of using "exactly from a given RV" semantics in the watchcache. [staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go] > That can be supported by etcd easily, just perform a quorum read and verify the resulting RV is recent enough.

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go] Re: backward incompatibility. The underlying issue here is that we have a single `storage.Interface` that is implemented with different RV semantics by `cacher.Cacher` (minimum RV semantics) than for `etcd.etcdHelper` and `etcd3.store` (exact RV semantics). This causes a couple problems:
 - We cannot document `storage.Interface`'s RV semantics since they're not consistent across implementations
 - Any new `storage.Interface` implementations must sort out what RV semantics is will expose and when if it's going to retain backward compatibility-- this interface doesn't allow for clean composition

Options for fixing this:
 1. Break backward compatibility- like discussed above. The scope of impact is clients of kubeapiserver's where the watchcache is disabled and that expect "exact RV" semantics (is this a very small/empty group?)
 2. Introduce a new `MinimumResourceVersion` field to `ListOptions` that is used for "minimum RV" semantics, mark `ResourceVersions` as deprecated and document that it has inconsistent semantics. This may also require making changes to storage.Interface since it currently only supports a single `ResourceVersion` param for many functions.

 I'm currently in favor of #1.

+import (
+	"fmt"
+	"io"
+	"os"
+	"path/filepath"
+)
+
+func copyFile(source, dest string) error {
+	sf, err := os.Open(source)
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("unable to open source file [%s]: %q", source, err)
+	}
+	defer sf.Close()
+	fi, err := sf.Stat()
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("unable to stat source file [%s]: %q", source, err)
+	}
+
+	dir := filepath.Dir(dest)
+	if err := os.MkdirAll(dir, 0755); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("unable to create directory [%s]: %q", dir, err)
+	}
+	df, err := os.Create(dest)
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("unable to create destination file [%s]: %q", dest, err)
+	}
+	defer df.Close()
+
+	_, err = io.Copy(df, sf)
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("unable to copy [%s] to [%s]: %q", source, dest, err)
+	}
+
+	if err := os.Chmod(dest, fi.Mode()); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("unable to close destination file: %q", err)
+	}
+	return nil
+}

human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go] how does this change behavior from a <= 1.16 client's perspective?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go] Basically it means that if Limit is set, only requests with RV="" will be served from etcd.
So what changes is:
- for requests with RV=value != {"", "0"} and Limit set, instead of 
  "exact RV="rv"" semantic, we get "at least RV="rv"" semantic

Which is consistent with what we document here:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#the-resourceversion-parameter

[and this is unrelated to client version - it impact clients in all versions the same way]
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go] This has the effect of no longer paging list requests like `?limit=500&resourceVersion=123`
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go] By serving from cache, doesn't this also change behavior of `limit=n,resourceVersion={non-0-value}` from "Exact" to "Not older than"?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go] > This has the effect of no longer paging list requests like ?limit=500&resourceVersion=123

Yes - that is true.
The question is who was using such requests (in k/k we started utilizing them with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83520, so in 1.17)

> By serving from cache, doesn't this also change behavior of limit=n,resourceVersion={non-0-value} from "Exact" to "Not older than"?

yeah - that's exactly what I wrote two comments above:

> for requests with RV=value != {"", "0"} and Limit set, instead of
"exact RV="rv"" semantic, we get "at least RV="rv"" semantic

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go] Also, since list resourceVersions can be obtained by a client via a list from etcd, and reflect the server's current version, but the resourceVersion observed by the server's storage cacher depends on having seen a resourceVersion in a watch event as part of an object change, this would make it possible for the apiserver to permanently time-out/reject list requests with valid resourceVersions

1. API server starts up, populates pod watch cache with a list at rv=10
2. Changes to pods happen at rv=11,12,13,14,15
3. API server watch cache observes those changes, sees "most recent rv" for pods as 15
4. Changes to configmaps occur at rv=16,17,18,19,20
5. Client does a list of `pods?resourceVersion=`, gets a current resource version of 20
6. Client uses that resourceVersion to do a list of `pods?limit=500&resourceVersion=20`, API server waits 3 seconds, then returns NewTooLargeResourceVersionError

It's not clear how a client in that scenario could make progress.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go] Agree that it's the problem - and that is one of the reasons this is market as WIP.
I wanted to evaluate performance of that (it seems that this is causing a lot of problem).

To solve this case, what i was thinking about was to:
- wait for some short amount of time (e.g. 1s or 500ms or sth) for the RV in cache
- if we didn't make enough progress, fallback to etcd

title: [WIP] Create CustomEncoder interface
human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] typo. s/inplement/ implement
[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] OnEncode? (just another idea for a name, not sure it's better)

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] I'm not a fan of OnEncode - this (by analogy to OnAdd/OnUpdate/OnDelete functions from informer frameworks) for me associates with "something happened and we can make additional action based on that". Which is not really the case here.

InterceptEncode (which BTW was also your suggestion - thanks!) I think is much better.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/json/json.go] how is the InterceptEncode method expected to make use of the injected encoder? if I'm following this correctly, it can't call `encoder.Encoder(self)` or we'll recurse. Does that mean every implementation of InterceptEncode must be implemented as a wrapper object around a normal encodable object?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/json/json.go] That was my intention - yes. Do you have a better suggestion to do that?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] I didn't expect a converter to be added here... this encoder's job is not to convert, just to set GVK, right?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] I'm not sure this interface is prescriptive enough. It exposes a lot of details about the encoder (presumably so the object can compute a cache key?), doesn't make it very clear what the object's responsibilities are, allows the called object to completely replace or modify the object passed to the encoder in cache miss cases, and also allows the called object to accidentally trigger an infinitely recursive call.

Rather than exposing details of the encoder, would it work to put the responsibility for computing a cache key on the encoder stack? I think a given encoder stack should be able to generate a cache key by accumulating the options of the delegates, like serialization (yaml, json, proto, etc), target version, etc.

Rather than implicitly relying on the interceptor to unwrap and pass back an encodeable object, should we make getting the encodeable object part of the interceptor interface?

```
type CacheableObject interface {
  ...
  GetEncodeableObject() runtime.Object
}
```

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] for an object that implements this interface, what would its implementation of DeepCopy() look like? would it preserve or discard the cached data?

how would we protect against this being accidentally used in code paths where objects are modified and serialized, and the modifications expected to be reflected in the serialized content?

how would we ensure that Encode() implementations that do type checks (for unstructured, etc) don't get bypassed by objects wrapped to implement caching/intercept interfaces?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] not really versioning Encoder is actually doing the conversion

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] Couple notes to myself so I don't forget to discuss tomorrow.
1. I initially thought that this might be great because it would mean that if we forget to handle the CacheableObject interface, then it can only be performance hit. But I'm not really sure if we can make that work so that serializing that object will result always in exactly the same format as the raw object to be serialized.
2. We would need to extend the interface of Encoder (or Serializer) to be able to return its options that uniquely identify it (e.g. yaml/json/proto, pretty, GV (for versioning), and so on. Is that acceptable?
3. For now I think the GetEncodeableObject() would need to probably take those options as a parameter - SelfLink is the reason [we send a single CacheableObject to all watchers, and conversions to different versions result in different selflinks]. [It also need to make a DeepCopy, but that seems to match the model].
4. We should forbid deep-copying of that object.
5. Modifying object is tricky: we can implement our own accessor for metadata and control it (or at least know that something went wrong), but should we also care about the rest of object? Can those be modified by something that is not an encoder?
6. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/response.go#L40 is what is tricky, because it's not even a serializer and it's manipulating objects
[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] Objects (like unstructured) could implement CacheableObject directly, and wouldn't have to unwrap themselves when invoking encode()

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] ```
  // Probably also
  GetObject(id SerializerIdentifier) runtime.Object
```

finding all the places that do typechecks and making sure they call this will be tricky. also, we shouldn't vary the encodeable object based on the serializer id, so probably no param is needed

[staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/helper.go] ```
CacheEncode(id SerializerIdentifier, encode func(runtime.Object, io.Writer)) ([]byte, error)
```

rather than getting back []byte, can we propagate the writer down so the object can stream to it

I thought it shouldn't be a problem because worst case we will loose a bit of work of processing something that noone will handle on the receiving end.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher_whitebox_test.go] This line can go into play in some tests - we should really be setting RV for all events...

Agree - although I think that's a separate thing and we shouldn't tightly couple these changes.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] I don't know enough about the edge cases of etcd deletion to know if it is possible for `txnResp.Responses` to be zero-length, or for `txnResp.Responses[0].GetResponseDeleteRange()` to return nil (the implementation certainly hints at the possibility)

Same question about the possibility of deleteResp.Header being nil

Can we be *very* defensive in what we assume about the etcd response here to avoid panics?

(xref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/76675/files#diff-c84f7808522d6cd14f52c2d800c897bbff103fcee2c73fa3bbb13da81db72298 as an example of rare edges in etcd responses)

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] I'd keep this one scoped narrowly to the code path being modified, and I wouldn't assume that responses to delete requests work the same way as responses to write requests. As far as I can see, this is the only path looking at GetResponseDeleteRange or pulling details out of a successful delete transation

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] This one, yes - I meant more broadly, if you are worried about edges (is it delete only, and if so, why?), I'm happy to pop in and handle the handful of cases where we index into `.Responses` and use those getters.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] Making these errors turns what would previously have been a successful delete response into an error. Is it better to error so callers don't get incorrect resourceVersions, or return origState.rev in this case so callers don't get errors?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] I was thinking about that, and my personal opinion is to rather return an error in this case.
I think that neither of these should generally happen looking at the implementation (though as you pointed out some corner cases are in theory possible).

But in those cases, I think it's better to error, than to send RV that would be misleading to users expect the semantic of "this is the current RV".

If you think very strongly the other way I can change that, but I think the current way is better (note that this code path is not used in watch, so it won't result in any broken watches or additional relists or anything like that - it's only the explicit Delete code path).

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] What would it even mean to get a successful transaction against etcd, with no response and no recorded delete? Would we even be certain that the deletion occurred? Would we try to undo it?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] I don't know what I don't know about possible etcd responses... is it documented what we can rely on from successful delete transactions? If non-nil/non-zero `.Responses[0].GetResponseDeleteRange().Header.Revision` is guaranteed, erroring here seems fine

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] The entirety of "documentation" here is the godoc on the `Responses` field:

```
	// responses is a list of responses corresponding to the results from applying
	// success if succeeded is true or failure if succeeded is false.
```

So if our transaction succeeded, and we asked for at least one key to be deleted, we can assume that there is at least one entry there. Barring a bug in `etcd` (is that what we're being defensive about?), we'd expect that response to be a delete response, as well, since that was the RPC we just used.

The response header is ubiquitous and must exist for RPCs, so similarly, barring a bug in `etcd` here, the chain `.Responses[0].GetResponseDeleteRange().Header.Revision` should never go out of bounds or nil panic.

To quote you from a different conversation:

> I want to make sure we're not adding new code that relies on an invariant the etcd API does not actually promise in a way that would turn previously 2xx operations into 5xx operations

To my reading, accessing the chain `.Responses[0].GetResponseDeleteRange().Header.Revision` here falls fully within the normal guarantees & expected behavior of `etcd`, so unless we *also* want to defend against bugs/places where these guarantees are not guaranteed by the type system, we should be fine without additional checks.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go] > So if our transaction succeeded, and we asked for at least one key to be deleted, we can assume that there is at least one entry there. Barring a bug in etcd (is that what we're being defensive about?), we'd expect that response to be a delete response, as well, since that was the RPC we just used.

+1 - the "correct behavior from etcd" (with our assumption from k8s that all our transactions add/update/delete exactly one object) is that we can expect that for delete transactions this `GetResponseDeleteRange()` to always be non-nil.
So we're rather protecting from bugs in etcd than any desired behavior here.


So I agree with @stevekuznetsov here - all those checks are rather protecting from bugs in etcd, than from a "correct behavior of etcd" - the correct behavior is that all of those should be set correctly and the newly added error-checking branches should never be called.

@liggitt - PTAL

human_review: [cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/options.go] LGTM, but can't we add a context to that queue that we can cancel?
[cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/options.go] what queue?

[cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/options.go] > what queue?

It's coming from SecureServingOptions::ApplyTo:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/serving.go#L266
which internally creates: DynamicServingContent:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/dynamiccertificates/dynamic_serving_content.go#L67
[which creates a queue]

But the trick is that any queue created by any component would behave exactly the same.


> but can't we add a context to that queue that we can cancel?

In theory we can add that, but usage of Queue is widely spread across the whole codebase:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ee0b179a7b9867203a9cc73f5c90909318a240e3/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/queue.go
and that would be a huge refactoring.
The additional problem is that most of our codebase is structured in a way:
- a method creating a certain object/controller
- `Run()` method that gets the context/stopCh that then closes everything it should 

The problem is when the creation method is spawning some goroutines, which is exactly the case for Queue, because Queue is initialized on creation (FWIW - it's also the case for almost every single controller we have - we just don't exercise the case when controllers are created by `Run()` method is not called, except from one testcase in `test/integration/serving`.

I fully agree it's not beautiful, but changing all of that would be on its own huge effort and I'm not convinced it's worth it.

[cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/options.go] I agree that we need a shorter-term solution (this PR).

I notice that the workqueue has a Shutdown method. We can possibly call that somewhere without having to introduce a context. It would have a lot of repeated code though :(

[cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/options.go] The Shutdown() method is called from Run() methods in all controllers.
The problem are those patological scenarios tested via this one test that is failing (and testing whether it fails) before Run() method is called.

We could in theory add a bunch of shutdowns everywhere - but that would be extremely ugly and error prone imho.

[cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/options.go] > I agree that we need a shorter-term solution (this PR).
> 
> I notice that the workqueue has a Shutdown method. We can possibly call that somewhere without having to introduce a context. It would have a lot of repeated code though :(

/hold cancel

the refactor is not likely going to happen soon 😄 
let´s move with the short term solution

Previously both items (prevStoredObj and storeObj) had the same key - the above PR broke it.
I'm fixing it in this PR.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] I shuffled the order of tests to force better testing of watchcache.

Basically when we were testing "resourceVersion=current" before "resourceVersion=previous", watchcache was synchronizing to "current" on the first testcase and was never on "previous" in the second one.
Changing the order means that for "previous" testcase it can actually be on both.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] key and prevKey were the same (before I broke it in [#113427](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113427)) and I fixed that again

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Can we randomize the keys used for the test, make each test case `t.Parallel()` and independent, and not allow them to influence each other?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Why do we want to change the semantic here? Channeling Jordan's conservative approach, even if the update flow in propagateStore is not needed, keeping it can't hurt, right?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] We should either be extremely explicit about the key, or always allow it to be generated. Not sure we gain a lot other than mental overhead by mixing the two.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] (or set random ns)

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] I don't understand your comment.

We're relying on the object namespace/name to be the key, so we're not mixing anything now.
Simply the rule is - the same object (defined by (namespace,name)) - same key, different object - different keys.

The rule is fairly explicit after the change from the previous PR.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] It's not what mattered here. What matter is that watchcache is not synchronous.

And I think for the semantic "NotOlderThan" it actually is fairly useful to test that semantic - for which the answer is not unique (if there were N changes after a given RV, all results are "correct" ones).

So I think that what we have currently is actually desired from the POV of testing the semantic of the interface.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] What I wanted to achieve is to get rid of "TestPropagateStoreWithKey" method - to really avoid confusion about the name...

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Sure, but it's implicit - I would walk in there and break it without having any idea! If we parallelized it and made cache hits from different tests independent, we could further write a test that's specific to the cache that does a number of calls in series, as the generic store interface doesn't provide any such guarantees, right?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Yes, I think now we're consistent as long as we're not specifying key but instead letting it be computed from the object being passed in.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Were getting rid of it to ensure that the key used in the store function calls is computed from the object (and thereby not suprising, etc), or something else?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] There are still few places which don't follow it, but I will be cleaning them in follow up PR.
But in general - this is exactly the direction I'm following.

IIRC - we're on the same page here, right?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Exactly (not all places were changed up until now, but this is the direction I'm heading.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] ohh - so you're effectively asking form actually running test cases in parallel? That sounds reasonable to me.

I was trying to make that happen by using t.Parallel() but I don't know how to make that work nicely...
As described in https://engineering.mercari.com/en/blog/entry/20220408-how_to_use_t_parallel/
t.Parallel() (for test subcases using t.Parallel()) are actually paused until the main test case finishes.
That makes the cleanup harder to run...

We can switch to t.Cleanup() in function calling those (from defer) which seems to work.
I'm not sure it's the nicest thing, but work.

I added that in a separate commit for now for you to take a look (and then even with the original order I can reproduce the problem of forgetting to add `prevStoredObj` as a correct result in
"existing key, resourceVersion=previous, resourceVersionMatch=notOlderThan" testcase.
[within 10 runs of tests]
Which is nice.

See the third commit if that's what you meant.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113645 is hopefully addressing all of that for store_tests.go
I will do a similar thing later for watcher tests too.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Sorry, so what I meant was a structure whereby each test case does it's own initialization - it can be a shared function similar to the current preamble - but by randomizing the namespace, we know we're independent in each test case, such that we don't have ordering dependencies that impact semantics of the test. Happy to tackle that in a follow-up if you'd like.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] I'm not sure we really need that - I think the single initialization we have here gives us enough.
The parallelization that I added (it's how I understood your comment, although it seems it wasn't exactly your intention) gives us additional benefit of testing potential races across multiple calls.
And it uncovers the races that I wanted to become visible.

The asynchronous nature of watchcache makes it likely to be hit by some potential nature, so making tests explicit that in some cases multiple answers are correct in some cases.

I think we may consider extending/improving this test in the future, but I think this PR is already visible improvement compared to the current state (better coverage), so I wouldn't block this PR on it. WDYT?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] I see, that makes sense - at least now we're not dependent on an implicit ordering of test cases to ensure we catch the behavior, but we will fail non-determinisitically instead. I think both approaches likely have merit, and I like being very explicit here, especially since the guarantees of the storage and the cache are slightly different, but at the least the current approach you have is not fragile like the first one, so I think this is sufficient, and yes, the current PR is a great improvement in and of itself.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Thanks - I agree it's not perfect and we can think later how to improve it further.

In the meantime, I will extend (in one of my future PRs) the comment explaining that a bit more in the code for posterity.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Why does adding a sleep cause the test to fail?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] was `RunTestGuaranteedUpdateWithSuggestionAndConflict` flaky or did you change it to match reality ?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] Without sleep, the list is happening before watchcache is initialized and was delegated to underlying storage.
If  watchcache is initialized, the this test is failing, because watchcache is ignoring Limit for RV=0.

We know that for RV=0, limit is ignored when used by watchcache - so yes, we want to test if for other RVs, it doesn't matter if its delegated or not, the result is the important stuff (but yes, it's delegated).

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing/store_tests.go] we're checking for non-0:

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go] I can believe it for the below section, but not for this bit running in a goroutine.

1. Imagine 3 successive calls A, B, C resulting in a run of this goroutine.
2. Call A happens first, takes the lock, and then the CPU context-switches away.
3. Then call B starts and blocks waiting for the lock.
4. Then call C starts and blocks waiting for the lock.
5. Then call A gets another timeslice, completes, and releases the lock.
6. Then call **C** acquires the lock and sets RV
7. Then call **B** acquires the lock and sets RV, making it go back in time.

+func (w *watchCache) suggestedWatchChannelSize(indexExists, triggerUsed bool) int {
+	// To estimate the channel size we use a heuristic that a channel
+	// should roughly be able to keep one second of history.
+	// We don't have an exact data, but given we store updates from
+	// the last <eventFreshDuration>, we approach it by dividing the
+	// capacity by the length of the history window.
+	chanSize := int(math.Ceil(float64(w.currentCapacity()) / eventFreshDuration.Seconds()))

+	// Finally we adjust the size to avoid ending with too low or
+	// to large values.
+	if chanSize < minWatchChanSize {
+		chanSize = minWatchChanSize
+	}
+	var maxChanSize int
+	switch {
+	case indexExists && triggerUsed:
+		maxChanSize = maxWatchChanSizeWithIndexAndTrigger
+	case indexExists && !triggerUsed:
+		maxChanSize = maxWatchChanSizeWithIndexWithoutTrigger
+	case !indexExists:
+		maxChanSize = maxWatchChanSizeWithoutIndex
+	}

+		chanSize = maxChanSize
+	}
+	return chanSize

title: Update the logic to pick the best queue in P&F
human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/fifo_list.go] nit: typo `seats`

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/fifo_list_test.go] can we also add a test for another form of idempotency - if we call both `RemoveFn` and `Dequeue` on the same request object, we expect the width to be decreased once.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/fifo_list.go] i don't think we need the lock, right? 
Where the FIFO is used, the calling function (`timeoutOldRequestsAndRejectOrEnqueueLocked` in this PR) already has acquired a lock on the queueset, so no other goroutine is accessing the queues at that point.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/fifo_list.go] yeah - good point

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/fifo_list.go] "Width" is a little awkward here, since the requests are generally not all run at the same time, so the sum of their widths is not a number of seats that gets occupied at once.  How about `SumOfSeats` or `SeatsSum`?

 	requestAbortsTotal.WithContext(req.Context()).WithLabelValues(reportedVerb, group, version, resource, subresource, scope).Inc()
 }
 
+// RecordDroppedRequest records that the request was rejected via http.TooManyRequests.
+func RecordDroppedRequest(req *http.Request, requestInfo *request.RequestInfo, component string, isMutatingRequest bool) {
+	if requestInfo == nil {
+		requestInfo = &request.RequestInfo{Verb: req.Method, Path: req.URL.Path}
+	}
+	scope := CleanScope(requestInfo)
+	dryRun := cleanDryRun(req.URL)
+
+	// We don't use verb from <requestInfo>, as this may be propagated from
+	// InstrumentRouteFunc which is registered in installer.go with predefined
+	// list of verbs (different than those translated to RequestInfo).
+	// However, we need to tweak it e.g. to differentiate GET from LIST.
+	reportedVerb := cleanVerb(CanonicalVerb(strings.ToUpper(req.Method), scope), getVerbIfWatch(req), req)
+
+	if requestInfo.IsResourceRequest {
+		requestCounter.WithContext(req.Context()).WithLabelValues(reportedVerb, dryRun, requestInfo.APIGroup, requestInfo.APIVersion, requestInfo.Resource, requestInfo.Subresource, scope, component, codeToString(http.StatusTooManyRequests)).Inc()
+	} else {
+		requestCounter.WithContext(req.Context()).WithLabelValues(reportedVerb, dryRun, "", "", "", requestInfo.Subresource, scope, component, codeToString(http.StatusTooManyRequests)).Inc()
+	}
+
+	if isMutatingRequest {
+		droppedRequests.WithContext(req.Context()).WithLabelValues(MutatingKind).Inc()
+	} else {
+		droppedRequests.WithContext(req.Context()).WithLabelValues(ReadOnlyKind).Inc()
+	}

title: Fix leaking goroutines coming from storage layer in integration tests
human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go] if CompleteWithOptions isn't called, or if s.Storage.Storage != nil, this won't register, right?
[test/integration/framework/controlplane_utils.go] nit: group imports

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go] I guess the same was already true of where we were registering inside the decorator

Do our destroy functions tolerate being called twice?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go] > if CompleteWithOptions isn't called, or if s.Storage.Storage != nil, this won't register, right?

Yes. The problem with the previous place in StorageWithCacher was that we were leaking other goroutines:
- if a resource wasn't using cacher (i.e. Events)
- the goroutine started from startObservingCount in this file

I agree that if CompleteWithOptions isn't called, it won't register, but this seems to be always called.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go] > Do our destroy functions tolerate being called twice?

Not everywhere:
- raw etcd3 storage can be called multiple times:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/storagebackend/factory/etcd3.go#L277
- cacher can be stopped multiple times: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L1008

- the stop from goroutine from startObservingCount can't be called twice:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go#L1471

Fixed the last one the same way it was previously addressed for etcd3 storage:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/storagebackend/factory/etcd3.go#L277

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] I suggest merging this PR with this as a "stop the bleeding" thing.

And I already have an opened WIP PR that is cleaning this up in: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109303 which we hopefully should be able to merge in 1.25 cycle.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] doesn't this mean we're double-registering and double cleaning-up? won't that make tests flake/fail if one test is cleaning up shared stuff while another test is in the middle of running?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] If we would be running multiple tests (within a single binary) at once, then yes.
In practice - we're running one at a time, and the reason it was needed was because of 4 tests that are also setting up aggregated apiserver, e.g. this one:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/integration/apiserver/apiserver_test.go#L831

- this is first setting up DefaultServer (L831)
- then setting up another apiserver (L837)

So this isn't a problem in our test setup.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] I really don't want to drop this protection unconditionally. I think it will be too easy to accidentally start two servers in parallel test runs and interfere with each other.

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] I would like to get rid of it completely very soon - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109303 is almost working.
Does it make sense to treat this PR as stop the bleeding? [If #109303 seems acceptable for you that this one would be very temporary].

The alternative would be to wait for the other one (though clearly it's too late for that on in 1.24)

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] FWIW - I have https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109303 already working and out for review - so if this isn't urgent (and given time in the release with every single it's being more clear that it should probably wait), we should probably switch to that other PR which is solving this problem in much cleaner way.

@liggitt - WDYT?
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] yeah, let's collapse onto that one.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go] OK - closing this one.

human_review: [pkg/controlplane/controller.go] we no longer fail if we don't allocate?

[pkg/controlplane/controller.go] Not explicitly, but we do implicitly.

So what happens, is that this Start (thanks to line 191: `wg.Wait()`) is synchronous in a sense that it waits until first attempt suceeds.
OTOH, Start() is called in pre-start-hook:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controlplane/controller.go#L149

So if we won't succeed, pre-start-hook doesn't succeed, so the cluster won't pass livez/ or readyz/ so in generall will get restarted by kubelet.

Does that make sense?

[pkg/controlplane/controller.go] yeah, but that assumes a containerized apiserver, a standalone binary will keep running ... I don't know if we should conservative, people using systemd per example for managing apiservers will face a different behavior?

[pkg/controlplane/controller.go] what about having a `RunOnceWait() <-chan struct`  instead of adding a function since we are only use this function for wait it runs once, we can use that to block and allows use to set a timeout
```
select {
case <- repairClusterIPs.RunOnceWait():
case <- time.After(15*time.Second):
       klog.Fatal()
}
```

[pkg/controlplane/controller.go] I personally feel that increasing the interface for the reason of somewhat artificial backward compatibility isn't worth it. I don't think we ever clearly document that we will fatal on if we can't repair even once at start.

human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go] does it means we start only once but we shutdown multiple times?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go] Sorry - maybe I wasn't clear.
What I meant is that:

- we create a separate QuotaEvaluator for every layer (separate for kube-apiserver, separate for agregated, separate for apiextensions)
- the creation of it actually creates a queue which starts a goroutine that is updating metrics (this is created in line 125 so once per quota evaluator)
- the newly added shutdownOnStop is also created here so called exactly once (per QuotaEvaluator)
- the start() is called *at most* once - line 606
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go] and why is not valid to keep it as it was?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go] Not sure I understand the question.

As I wrote above - when I create QuotaEvaluator, this is underneath starting a gorotuine (created by `workqueue.NewNamed`).
That goroutine is shut down only when run() (renamed to start()) method is called.

run() is called on the first `Evaluate` - if that is not called - the goroutine will be leaked.
[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go] ahhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh ... sorry friday and lack coffeeeeeee

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go] This is good question.
From one hand, this is what users get when the list from etcd (etcd returns a sorted list of results). Given that this was original semantic, people may potentially be used for it.
OTOH - it clearly wasn't the case in watchcache, since it was created. Given that noone realized this discrepancy, it may also mean that it's not a critical feature. [pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go] This is obviously not the right way of doing that, as we can't change defaults.

The question is how exactly we should do that:
- we seem to already have v1 API, but that don't even have any defaulting:
 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1
- given the config is already in v1 - what options do we have to change it?

[pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go] I'm not sure this is so terrible in a config type?

Do you want to remove the limit or increase it a lot? At 1k you might as well remove it completely?

In that case an alternative could be to add a "UseRateLimit" field and default it to false?

I'd get kubelet authors to weigh in first.

[pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go] I don’t know why we wouldn’t go to 25 or 50 as a first step, then a release later with soak jump another bit.  I struggle to think of kubelet even on 512 pod nodes being able to saturate 50qps anyway

[pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go] > I struggle to think of kubelet even on 512 pod nodes being able to saturate 50qps anyway

For extended period of time - I agree. As a spike - I actually can - let's say some large pod just finished there and we have a place to start next new small 30 pods, with 10 secrets each. That gives O(400) API calls...

That said - I would be fine with doing it in steps, if it's not a big overhead like creating a new config version to avoid changing defaults within a single (group, version) or sth.

[pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go] When I looked at this for EKS, I found that I got most of the benefit just by doubling the QPS/burst.  We've used 10 QPS 20 Burst as the default kubelet values for EKS AMIs since K8s 1.22. I'm happy to see the defaults increased.

The below graph is 3k pods and 30 nodes showing time to pod readiness.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/64753/222772332-0cd7a550-1736-42b9-8ad2-e839f56d94fd.png)

The other situation where it helps is in auto-scaling.  E.g. New pods are created, causing new nodes to be launched and large numbers of pods then schedule to the same node at roughly the same time as it goes ready.


Refs:
- https://github.com/awslabs/amazon-eks-ami/pull/1030
- https://github.com/bottlerocket-os/bottlerocket/pull/2436

[pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go] >  At 1k you might as well remove it completely?

I think having a safeguard at a very high, but not extremely high value would protect API server from errors in kubelet. Virtually unlimited normal operation sounds reasonable to me.

@wojtek-t when I looked yesterday I thought the limit increased to 100/500. I might not remember correctly since I don't se force push there =). For me 100/500 was the good first step as @smarterclayton suggested.

One risk of 1k is potentially we can make kubelet to become a noisy neighbor in the moment of rescheduling (like @wojtek-t described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116121#discussion_r1124679953 with 400 requests). It may be a problem when there are other API server clients on the node or network is very limited and close to be saturated... But we are keeping configuration settings and for set ups with limited network connectivity one can change defaults back.

Currently there are two separate mechanisms that are implemented:
- "progress notify" - it's an etcd feature that where etcd sends a bookmark with current (global) RV if no objects within the scope of the watch changed in the last N seconds

What I meant in my previous comment is that for watchlist request we cannot guarantee the ordering. The following order is possible:
1. the watchcache is behind etcd, say etcd is at rv=5 and the watchcache is at rv=4, so `bookmarkAfterRV=5`
2. we have the `watchCacheEvent` with the following keys (init events): `foo`, `bar`
3. we sort the init events and we get `bar`, `foo`
4. we send the init events to a client
5. at some point we get a new event with the following key `baz` at `rv=5`
6. we send the newly received event to the client followed by the special bookmark event

at the client-side we received events in the following order: `bar`, `foo`, `baz` whereas the desired order was `bar`, `baz`, `foo`.

human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] (and if we separately made our in-tree use of transformer idempotent, we'd avoid data race risks as well and that could maybe be narrowly picked to 1.29.x and 1.30.1 faster)

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] Done

And I will open a separate PR to make the functions idempotent.

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] I'm a little wary of this constraint. Consumers of the `TransformFunc` will not be aware of nor have control over how or where the object they receive came from. Nor should they care - that's an implementation detail of the `DeltaFIFO`. Also the `DeltaFIFO` itself does not have control over the origin of the objects from the upstream informers. I think it would be ideal for the `DeltaFIFO` to provide protection for the `TransformFunc` from potential data races. If an object already exists in the `knownObjects` cache and, more specifically, points to the same **instance** then make a copy of it before passing to the `TransformFunc`. The `TransformFunc` would then truly be free to mutate the object w/o any additional idempotency constraint. In fact we could go a step further and elide invoking the `TransformFunc` altogether in this case since we know the object came from the cache and was already transformed. Then we wouldn't really even need to special-case the tombstone or `Sync` action.

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] I agree that preventing more races is desired, however these for now these don't expose default usage of it. We should protect it further, but preventing existing issues seems more important to start with.

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] > however these for now these don't expose default usage of it.

I'm not clear on what you mean by this.

I think the text above would be a bit vague and confusing to users of the API. It would be for me if I hadn't studied the code and understand the issue and what it's trying say. With the changes in this PR, the potential race issue with passing cached objects to the `DeltaFIFO` could only occur with a custom informer and it's probably unlikely anyone is doing that so I'd omit this text. In fact, this should really documented as part of the `DeltaFIFO` API.
[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] can delete this sentence fragment, the DeletedFinalStateUnknown bit no longer applies

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] >> however these for now these don't expose default usage of it.
>
> I'm not clear on what you mean by this.

After the fix in this PR to omit Sync events and DeletedFinalStateUnknown objects, none of the uses of DeltaFIFO that client-go sets up (default informers / clients, etc) feed objects already present in `knownObjects` back into the transformer.

That means the only way a DeltaFIFO user would encounter that is if they wired up a non-default usage of DeltaFIFO to pass the same objects into DeltaFIFO multiple times as if they were new objects.

Someone doing that is presumably the same person wiring up the TransformFunc, and they need to understand the implications of what they are doing. Doing this effectively already breaks the *TransformFunc sees the object before any other actor, and it is now safe to mutate the object in place instead of making a copy.* statement / guarantee, so the TransformFunc author _must_ be aware of the implications of mutating objects it gets when they are being provided by something with different behavior than default client-go clients / informers.

> If an object already exists in the `knownObjects` cache and, more specifically, points to the same **instance** then make a copy of it before passing to the `TransformFunc`

The tracking / comparison cost to safeguard `TransformFunc` in that case is too high, and even if we did, `TransformFunc` would have to be aware of and protect against disrupting a non-default object provider.

[staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/delta_fifo.go] I understand the reasoning. My point is that the `TransformFunc` is part of a higher-level API and is much more widely used and visible then the `DeltaFIFO`. The `New*Informer` functions are really the external-facing aspect of the `cache` module and I'm sure most users of these aren't even aware of `DeltaFIFO` and its semantics (I wasn't until I investigated this issue). As you mentioned, the author of a non-default usage of `DeltaFIFO`, if there are any, is "_presumably the same person wiring up the TransformFunc_", therefore document the constraints and implications re: caching and the `TransformFunc` in the `DeltaFIFO` API rather than here. This makes sense b/c the constraint that the `TransformFunc` be idempotent only applies if a non-default `DeltaFIFO` producer is used. As I said, I think the paragraph above will only confuse most people. Anyway, that's my 2 cents...

human_review: [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go] Is this concern for Replace invalid? Or do we need to consider it?

[staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go] I no longer understand this comment (even though I was the one who added this).

But the story for replace is the following:
- we're using reflector and it's reflector that is calling the Replace
- the way reflector works is that it's effectively single-threaded - it's either processing watch events (and calling Add/Modify/Delete functions which land here) or calling Replace (and then this function can't be called).

So this safe.


The only interpretation that comes to my mind is that I had in mind some generic usage of watchcache, where the functions aren't called from reflector but by some arbitrary caller in arbitrary order from multiple threads. In such case this change wouldn't be safe, but it's not how it is used.

But in general, mutating `s` here in the config constructor has smell (unexpected side-effect). 

The cleaner solution, and question is whether there are other ripples, would be to move this kind of cross-options logic into the option completion func, i.e. here for controlplane/apiserver that would be https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95d71c464a6a5f81ae36bddc86972b3b2a1c40a5/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/options/options.go#L206.

[pkg/controlplane/apiserver/config.go] The pattern is always:

NewOptions, tweak values, AddFlags(), evaluate flags, Complete().
NewConfig(options), tweak values, Complete().
NewServer(config), tweak values, Complete(), PrepareRun(), Run().

The `Complete()` func is where you add defaulting, or cross options logic. Every constructor is side-effect-free.

[pkg/registry/scheduling/workload/strategy.go] > all the code handling a given field should effectively get disabled too

FTR that isn't really how we implement Gates.  You called out some of the reasons for it, but the usual implementation is that the gate controls the "front door", which is the API.  If a configuration has made it through the front door, then we usually respect it.  I know it seems counterintuitive, that the feature gate is disabled and yet the feature is working, but it's the only way to implement many of our gated features. 

Like you said, and enum with a new value is a good example.  Are we supposed to assume a different value when the gate is closed after use? That seems hostile and confusing.  We are certainly not going to mutate the object just because the future gate is disabled.

Or consider features which have some "running" state, like kubelet writing to a c group file.  That may not be modifiable, whether the gate is enabled or not.

So, almost always, the guidance for feature Gates is that the gate prevents activation of the feature via the API, but if the feature is activated, the logic should handle it. What that practically means is that API controlled logic generally shouldn't even check the feature gate. 

There is some leeway as to to a user should be able to change API values if the feature was already enabled, or if they're just stuck using the configuration they have. That's what this is about. 

I am fine to say that they cannot change the value, but if the value is set, the system should probably use it.  Otherwise the API says one thing, but the system is doing something else. 

There is so much variance between features, that it's hard to make a single rule that covers all cases.

[pkg/registry/scheduling/workload/strategy.go] > FTR that isn't really how we implement Gates. If a configuration has made it through the front door, then we usually respect it. I know it seems counterintuitive, that the feature gate is disabled and yet the feature is working, but it's the only way to implement many of our gated features.

So it heavily depends on the feature. For many features that drive e.g. certain behavior in controllers (e.g. new upgrade strategy of statefulset, etc.) we actually gate the actual behavior also with the gate.

The same will be done in scheduler - if the FG is disabled, we will not be preempting PodGroups as a whole (even if they have disruption mode set accordingly).

Apparently it seems we're heavily inconsistent across the project.

[pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dra_manager.go] Note that the problem we're trying to solve is multi-layer:
1. Scheduling Pods within a PodGroup in a single cycle
2. Re-scheduling the same PodGroups across many scheduling cycles (mainly Basic gang smaller minCount)
3. Scheduling different Pods (sharing the same Claim) across different cycles
4. Scheduling different PodGroups (sharing the same Claim) across different cycles

We need to solve the case 1, but we ended up solving all other case 2 - 4. This is fine as the difference between them is not big, as even in the case 1 we still have sync (PreFilter, Reserve, Unreserve) and async (Bind, Unreserve) phases. But the question is whether we want to worry about the allocations crafted in the previous cycle which haven't bound yet (or fail binding)?

+	"k8s.io/kubernetes/test/integration/framework"
+	"k8s.io/kubernetes/test/utils/kubeconfig"
+)
+
+// TestLeaderElectionReleaseOnCancel verifies that when the
+// ControllerManagerReleaseLeaderElectionLockOnExit feature gate is enabled,
+// tearing down the KCM (cancelling its context) causes the leader election
+// lease to be released (holder identity cleared). This allows a new leader
+// to acquire the lock without waiting for the full lease duration to expire.
+//
+// Note: We only test the feature-enabled case here. The feature-disabled case
+// retains the legacy behavior where OnStoppedLeading calls klog.FlushAndExit
+// (os.Exit), which cannot be tested in-process.
+func TestLeaderElectionReleaseOnCancel(t *testing.T) {
+	// Start a real API server.
+	apiServer := kubeapiservertesting.StartTestServerOrDie(t, nil, framework.DefaultTestServerFlags(), framework.SharedEtcd())
+	t.Cleanup(apiServer.TearDownFn)
+
+	client, err := kubernetes.NewForConfig(apiServer.ClientConfig)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("failed to create client: %v", err)
+	}
+
+	// Write a kubeconfig file for the KCM to use.
+	clientConfig := kubeconfig.CreateKubeConfig(apiServer.ClientConfig)
+	kubeConfigFile := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "kubeconfig.yaml")
+	if err := clientcmd.WriteToFile(*clientConfig, kubeConfigFile); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("failed to write kubeconfig: %v", err)
+	}
+
+	// Start a full KCM with leader election and the feature gate enabled.
+	ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
+	defer cancel()
+
+	kcm, err := kubecontrollermanagertesting.StartTestServer(t, ctx, []string{
+		"--kubeconfig=" + kubeConfigFile,
+		"--leader-elect=true",
+		"--feature-gates=ControllerManagerReleaseLeaderElectionLockOnExit=true",
+	})
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("failed to start KCM: %v", err)
+	}
+	t.Cleanup(kcm.TearDownFn)
+
+	// Wait for the lease to exist and have a holder. There can be a brief gap
+	// between the KCM's /healthz becoming ready and the lease being acquired.
+	var lease *coordinationv1.Lease
+	err = wait.PollUntilContextTimeout(context.Background(), 100*time.Millisecond, 30*time.Second, true, func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) {
+		lease, err = client.CoordinationV1().Leases("kube-system").Get(ctx, "kube-controller-manager", metav1.GetOptions{})
+		if err != nil {
+			return false, nil // retry on not-found or transient errors
+		}
+		return lease.Spec.HolderIdentity != nil && *lease.Spec.HolderIdentity != "", nil
+	})
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("timed out waiting for lease to have a holder: %v", err)
+	}
+	t.Logf("lease holder before shutdown: %q", *lease.Spec.HolderIdentity)
+
+	// Tear down the KCM (cancels its context), which should release the lease.
+	kcm.TearDownFn()
+
+	// Poll until the lease holder is cleared.
+	err = wait.PollUntilContextTimeout(context.Background(), 100*time.Millisecond, 10*time.Second, true, func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) {
+		lease, err = client.CoordinationV1().Leases("kube-system").Get(ctx, "kube-controller-manager", metav1.GetOptions{})
+		if err != nil {
+			return false, err
+		}
+		return lease.Spec.HolderIdentity == nil || *lease.Spec.HolderIdentity == "", nil
+	})
+	if err != nil {
+		holder := "<nil>"
+		if lease.Spec.HolderIdentity != nil {
+			holder = *lease.Spec.HolderIdentity
+		}
+		t.Fatalf("expected lease holder to be cleared after shutdown, but got %q: %v", holder, err)
+	}
+	t.Log("lease holder cleared after shutdown")
+}

There is already a PR in-flight that adds protection controller: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137641 which effectively means:
1) we will be adding a finalizer on the PodGroup on its creation
2) the finalizer will be removed only when all pods referencing it will move to the terminated state (or get deleted)

Even if we have that, we don't have guarantee that the last Pod (which was supposed to remove the PodGroup) won't be deleted, so won't trigger PodGroup removal (deleted pod cannot trigger scheduler action).
